CHAPITRE 5. INVERSER L’IRRIGATION À PARTIR DE DONNÉES D’HUMIDITÉ DU 88                                                      SOL DE SURFACE [SOURCE: Page_100]

36   1 Introduction [SOURCE: Page_100]

37   Irrigation is the most water-intensive human activity, consuming more than 70% of the freshwater used worldwide (Foley 38   et al., 2011; Qin et al., 2019). Pressure on water resources already exists in many regions and is expected to increase in 39   the future (Wada et al., 2011, 2013; Campbell et al., 2017; FAO, 2021). This is largely due to the combined effect of 40   increased food demand associated with economic and population growth (Tilman & Clark, 2015), and the impact of 41   climate change on hydrometeorological response (Ferguson et al., 2018; Malek et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2020). To 42   best manage this situation, decision makers, including water resource managers need to know how much water is being 43   used for irrigation, at regional (irrigation district, catchment), national and global scales (OECD, 2015). However, access 44   to reliable information on irrigation water use is currently lacking. It either does not exist, or is subject to large 45   uncertainties    inherent   in   national    or   international    databases,       such   as   the   AQUASTAT       dataset 46   (http://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/; accessed 16 June 2023) (Ajaz et al., 2020; Puy et al., 2022a), or in the predictions of 47   hydrological models (Wada et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2018; Puy et al., 2022b). Indeed, models generally simulate 48   irrigation based on empirically defined soil moisture thresholds, which are highly variable in space and time and therefore 49   highly uncertain (Olivera-Guerra et al., 2023). In addition, irrigation modeling is affected by other sources of uncertainty, 50   such as irrigated area or irrigation efficiency (Puy et al., 2021, 2022a, 2022b). [SOURCE: Page_100]

51   While the need for knowledge of irrigation water use is growing, and the irrigation models are still too uncertain to meet 52   the challenge, more and more remote sensing observations relevant to irrigation retrieval are becoming freely available. 53   Over the last two decades, the number of satellites carrying solar and thermal spectrum sensors (e.g., Moderate resolution 54   Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), Landsat, Sentinel-2 (S$_2$), Sentinel-3) from which evapotranspiration (ET) products 55   can be derived (such as SEN-ET; Guzinski et al., 2020), and passive (e.g., Soil Moisture and Ocean Salinity (SMOS), 56   Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP)) and active microwave (e.g., Advanced SCATterometer (ASCAT), Sentinel-1 (S$_1$)) 57   sensors, from which soil moisture products can be derived (e.g., El Hajj et al., 2017; Ojha et al., 2019; Paolini et al., 58   2022), has steadily increased. This opens up increasingly interesting possibilities in terms of spatial and temporal 59   resolution (Peng et al., 2021). The wealth of information available from remote sensing has led to the emergence of a 60   community of researchers focused on irrigation estimation from satellite observations. Massari et al. (2021) recently 61   provided an overview of the various existing approaches based on satellite observations. [SOURCE: Page_100]

62   Some of these works have attempted to retrieve irrigation by comparing the remotely sensed ET of two (one irrigated and 63   one rainfed) neighboring crops (e.g., Romaguera et al., 2014; Vogels et al., 2020) or by assuming that it corresponds to 64   the difference between simulated and remotely sensed ET (e.g., Anderson et al., 2015; López Valencia et al., 2020). In 65   the same vein, Zhang and Long (2021) have retrieved monthly irrigation at the scale of US states by exploiting the 66   difference between simulated and remotely sensed ET, by relying on a linear relationship between ET and root zone soil 67   moisture. However, all of these ET-based methods suffer from the same pitfall. The information contained in ET 68   observations is limited to the water actually consumed by the crop fields, thus neglecting any excess water applied 69   intentionally (e.g., to allow soil leaching) or unintentionally (due to suboptimal practices). Assuming that ET data can be 70   used to determine the irrigation actually applied is equivalent to assuming that farmers never irrigate more than the crop 71   can consume. However, over-irrigation may occur. This can be observed, for example, in the Algerri-Balaguer (AB) 72   irrigation district in northeastern Spain, where the observed drainage (related to excess water in the soil) occurs mainly 73   in summer, when irrigation is intensive and rainfall is low (Altès et al., 2022; Laluet et al., 2023b). [SOURCE: Page_100]

5.5. ARTICLE. RETRIEVING THE IRRIGATION ACTUALLY APPLIED AT DISTRICT SCALE : ASSIMILATING HIGH-RESOLUTION SENTINEL-1-DERIVED SOIL MOISTURE DATA INTO A FAO-56-BASED MODEL                                      89 [SOURCE: Page_101]

74    Many other recently published approaches propose to estimate irrigation using the surface soil moisture (SSM) data 75    derived from microwave observations. Remotely sensed SSM can detect the irrigation signal (Le Page et al., 2020; 76    Jalilvand et al., 2021; Lawston, et al., 2017) and theoretically both under-irrigation (below the amount of water needed to 77    avoid crop stress) and over-irrigation (above the amount of water the soil can hold, resulting in drainage). An irrigation 78    retrieval model based on SSM data was proposed by Brocca et al. (2018) using the SM2RAIN approach. It has since been 79    used in various works (e.g., Jalilvand et al., 2019; Dari et al., 2020, 2022, 2023; Filippucci et al., 2020). SM2RAIN relies 80    on a simple water balance equation whose terms depend on observed SSM and empirical parameters, which are previously 81    calibrated over rainfed areas or during periods when there is no irrigation. Jalilvand et al. (2019) applied this method 82    using SSM data from the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer 2 (AMSR$_2$; ~25 km resolution) over an irrigation 83    district in Iran. Although the overall irrigation dynamics was well reproduced, irrigation was systematically 84    overestimated. By applying a bias correction obtained from the application of SM2RAIN over rainfed areas, the results 85    were significantly improved with a root mean square deviation (RMSD) of 13 mm month-1. They highlighted the 86    sensitivity of irrigation to the ET formalism and emphasized the need to use SSM observations at higher spatial resolution. 87    Later, Dari et al. (2020) and (2022) applied the same approach to semi-arid irrigation districts in Spain at a finer spatial 88    resolution using the SMOS and SMAP SSM data disaggregated at 1 km resolution (DISPATCH SSM datasets; Merlin et 89    al., 2013). They showed that an improved formulation of ET (particularly using the FAO-56 approach of Allen et al., 90    1998) significantly improves irrigation retrievals. This highlights the importance of properly representing the processes 91    involved in the crop water balance. [SOURCE: Page_101]

92   Recently, Dari et al. (2023) used SM2RAIN with S$_1$ and Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (CYGNSS) derived 93   SSM products (1 km and 6 km spatial resolution, respectively) on ten irrigation districts in Spain, Italy, and Australia. 94   The retrieved irrigation reproduces in situ observations well, but with sometimes significant biases, especially for small 95   irrigation districts. In fact, all the papers involving SM2RAIN have emphasized the importance of using a high-resolution 96   SSM product to detect processes occurring at the field scale. In parallel with these works, Zappa et al. (2021) proposed 97   an approach close to SM2RAIN, called SM_Delta, based on the comparison of SSM variation between an irrigated pixel 98   and the rainfed pixels surrounding it. Zappa et al. (2022) evaluated the performance of this approach on synthetic data 99   and showed that it is highly sensitive to both spatial resolution and observation frequency. Performance declines sharply 100   for periods of more than three days between two consecutive SSM observations, and when the irrigated fraction of a pixel 101   falls below 70%. This illustrates the importance of high-resolution observations capable of providing pixels with a high 102   irrigation fraction. [SOURCE: Page_101]

103   In addition to the issues of spatial resolution and revisit time of SSM datasets, another limitation of current SSM-based 104   approaches such as SM2RAIN is that they neglect the issue of uncertainty, whether caused by the model (uncertainty in 105   model parameters and formalism) or by satellite observations (uncertainty in input data). However, all models are 106   sensitive to the choices made in the calibration step, to the model formalism and parameterization, and to the uncertainty 107   of its input data (Foster et al., 2020; Beven et al., 2019; Puy et al., 2022b). Knowledge of the uncertainty in the model 108   estimate is actually as important as the modeled value to provide reliable information to decision makers and managers 109   (Saltelli et al., 2020). [SOURCE: Page_101]

110   Other approaches based on the assimilation of satellite SSM data into land surface models (LSMs) have recently been 111   developed, enabling uncertainty to be taken into account in irrigation simulations. Assimilation methods are based on the 112   prior distributions of both model and observational errors. Felfelani et al. (2018) assimilated SMAP (36 km spatial [SOURCE: Page_101]

CHAPITRE 5. INVERSER L’IRRIGATION À PARTIR DE DONNÉES D’HUMIDITÉ DU 90                                                      SOL DE SURFACE [SOURCE: Page_102]

113   resolution) SSM data into the Community Land Model version-4.5 LSM (Lawrence et al., 2011; Oleson et al., 2013) over 114   a large irrigated area in the USA, using the one-dimensional Kalman filter method. The goal was to constrain the so- 115   called "target soil moisture" parameter, which determines the irrigation triggering and amount. They obtained a significant 116   improvement in the simulated annual irrigation compared to the baseline simulation performed using the default parameter 117   value. In the same vein, Abolafia-Rosenzweig et al. (2019) inverted irrigation amounts by assimilating (synthetic) SSM 118   data into the variable infiltration capacity LSM using the particle batch smoother data assimilation approach. The results 119   of the twin experiment indicated that the assimilation approach is better when the timing of irrigation is known, and when 120   the revisit time of the SSM observation is less than three days. They also highlighted the importance of addressing the 121   issue of persistent biases between simulated and observed SSM. Jalilvand et al. (2023) applied the same approach but 122   using the 1 km resolution SMAP-S$_1$ SSM data (Das et al., 2019) over an irrigation district in Iran. They confirmed the 123   importance of an a priori knowledge of irrigation frequencies in their approach and obtained an underestimation of 124   seasonal cumulative irrigation at the irrigated pixels by an average of 19%, explained by the loss of irrigation signal due 125   to the mismatch between the spatial resolution (1 km) of the SSM data and the scale of irrigation practices. [SOURCE: Page_102]

126   Modanesi et al. (2022) assimilated the S$_1$ backscatter (aggregated to 1 km resolution) to improve the performance of the 127   Noah-MP.v.3.6 LSM (Niu et al., 2011) coupled with an irrigation module (Ozdogan et al., 2010a), using an ensemble 128   Kalman filter. The assimilation resulted in an improvement of the simulated irrigation, but to a limited extent. In 129   particular, they emphasized the importance of dealing with observations and simulations at higher spatial resolution (with 130   low performance when pixel had low irrigation fraction), as well as the need for more frequent SSM observations and 131   improvement of the Noah-MP.v.3.6 irrigation module formalism. At a finer spatial scale, Ouaadi et al. (2021) estimated 132   the timing and amount of irrigation for five wheat plots in Morocco. They assimilated a high-resolution (15 m, revisit 133   time of six days) SSM product derived from S$_1$ into a model based on the FAO-56 method, using the particle filter (PF) 134   approach (Vrugt et al., 2013). PF is one of the most efficient assimilation methods, able to take into account for model 135   and observational uncertainties without the need for any assumptions about prior density functions or likelihoods and is 136   adapted to nonlinear problems (unlike 4DVar or Kalman filter-based methods) (van Leeuwen et al., 2019; Alonso- 137   González et al., 2022). For all five plots, Ouaadi et al. (2021) obtained a Pearson correlation coefficient r of 0.64 and an 138   RMSD of 28.7 mm/15 days and were able to detect 50-70% of irrigation events. They also showed, using in situ data, 139   that their approach performed better with a shorter revisit time (three days). [SOURCE: Page_102]

140   A recurring issue in assimilation approaches is the management of persistent differences between modeled and observed 141   SSM. To reduce model or observation biases, one possible solution is to use a rescaling approach such as cumulative 142   distribution function matching (Reichle and Koster., 2004) to fit the observed SSM to the simulated SSM. However, this 143   approach has the disadvantage of potentially deleting signals when the observations contain some information that is not 144   modeled, such as irrigation (Kumar et al., 2015; Nair and Indu, 2019). Another way to minimize such a bias is to calibrate 145   model parameters on rainfed pixels (e.g., Dari et al., 2020, 2022; Jalilvand et al., 2023), although this implies the strong 146   (and unverified) assumption that optimal parameters for rainfed pixels are also optimal for irrigated pixels. Another 147   approach is to remove a systematic bias (calculated on rainfed pixels) from the simulated irrigations (Jalilvand et al., 148   2019), although part of the signal may be lost due to the difference in climatology or soil properties between both pixel 149   types (Brombacher et al., 2022). [SOURCE: Page_102]

150   The above literature review of SSM-based irrigation retrieval methods indicates that state-of-the-art approaches are 151   currently limited by (one or several of the following factors): 1) the coarse resolution of SSM remote sensing products [SOURCE: Page_102]

4 [SOURCE: Page_102]

5.5. ARTICLE. RETRIEVING THE IRRIGATION ACTUALLY APPLIED AT DISTRICT SCALE : ASSIMILATING HIGH-RESOLUTION SENTINEL-1-DERIVED SOIL MOISTURE DATA INTO A FAO-56-BASED MODEL                                      91 [SOURCE: Page_103]

152   used as input, 2) the impact of data gaps in SSM time series due to low revisit, 3) the non-explicit representation of 153   irrigation-related (e.g., ET, deep percolation, etc.) processes which makes the calibration steps difficult and uncertain, 154   and 4) the lack of consideration (by the irrigation retrieval methods that are not based on data assimilation) of uncertainties 155   in both model parameterization and input data. [SOURCE: Page_103]

156   In this context, this study proposes a new assimilation scheme of a high (15 m) resolution S$_1$-derived SSM product 157   (Ouaadi et al., 2020) into the FAO-56-based crop water balance model SAtellite Monitoring for IRrigation (SAMIR; 158   Simonneaux et al., 2009), using the PF method. The SAMIR model, implemented at the field scale, allows for a robust 159   and explicit representation of crop ET from the crop coefficient values available for all common crops for different 160   climates in the FAO-56 look-up tables. It can therefore be spatialized over large areas from readily available data (Laluet 161   et al., 2023b). In addition, the assimilation approach developed by Olivera-Guerra et al. (2023) is used here to invert two 162   parameters of the SAMIR irrigation module: the irrigation amount (Idose) and the soil moisture threshold (SMthreshold) at 163   which irrigation is triggered. Both parameters are retrieved over successive monthly assimilation windows integrating 164   several (up to five independent) S$_1$-derived SSM observations. Such a strategy helps to reduce the impact of possible data 165   gaps in SSM time series and allows for representing weekly district-scale water use in any (deficit, full or excess) irrigation 166   regime (Olivera-Guerra et al., 2023). [SOURCE: Page_103]

167   The proposed approach is implemented over the 8000 hectare AB irrigation district located in northeastern Spain. It is 168   evaluated at the field and AB scales using in situ irrigation measurements available at both scales. The paper is organized 169   as follows: Section 2 presents the study area and the data used, Section 3 introduces the SAMIR model and its irrigation 170   module (Section 3.1), as well as the assimilation scheme (Section 3.2), the strategy for performing plot-scale simulations 171   (Section 3.3), and the evaluation step (Section 3.4). Section 4 presents and discusses the results obtained first at the field 172   scale using in situ SSM data as input (Section 4.1), and then at the AB district scale using S$_1$-derived SSM data as input 173   (Section 4.2). Section 5 presents conclusions and perspectives of this work. [SOURCE: Page_103]

174 175   2 Study area and data [SOURCE: Page_103]

176   2.1 Study area [SOURCE: Page_103]

177   The study area is the 8000 hectare AB irrigation district located in northeastern Spain, 20 km north of the city of Lleida. 178   The climate is continental Mediterranean with an average annual reference evapotranspiration (ET$_0$) of 1027 mm and 179   rainfall of 380 mm (2000-2021). For the year 2019, 6140 hectares were irrigated, of which 94% were covered by five 180   main crop types: double crops (62% of the irrigated area; mainly barley or wheat in winter-spring season and maize in 181   summer-fall), summer cereals (9%; maize), winter cereals (8%; mainly barley or wheat), forages (8%; mainly alfalfa), 182   and fruit trees (7%). The remaining 6% are composed of leguminous, oleaginous, horticultural and protein crops, as well 183   as vineyards and olive trees. All the plots are irrigated by sprinklers (in summer the daily doses range from 5 to 15 mm), 184   except for the fruit trees, which are irrigated by drip irrigation. The land use information used in this study comes from 185   the Geographic Information System for Agricultural Parcels (SIGPAC), provided by the Department of Climate Action, 186   Food,      and     Rural      Agenda       of      the     Region       of     Catalonia,      and     is     available      at 187   https://agricultura.gencat.cat/ca/ambits/desenvolupamentrural/sigpac/descarregues (accessed 16 June 2023). Figure 1.a 188   shows the AB district with the land cover for the year 2019 from the SIGPAC database. [SOURCE: Page_103]

5 [SOURCE: Page_103]

CHAPITRE 5. INVERSER L’IRRIGATION À PARTIR DE DONNÉES D’HUMIDITÉ DU 92                                                      SOL DE SURFACE [SOURCE: Page_104]

189 190   Figure 1: The AB irrigation district with the land cover for the year 2019, the location of the pumping station and of the 191   two instrumented plots (Albesa and Castello) (a), and the weekly irrigation data measured at the pumping station in 2019 192   (b) (coordinates of the pumping station: 797157/4636983.4 ETRS89/UTM zone 31N). [SOURCE: Page_104]

193 194   2.2 In situ data [SOURCE: Page_104]

195   2.2.1 District-scale in situ irrigation data [SOURCE: Page_104]

196   The district-scale irrigation data consists of the water flow pumped in the river Noguera Ribagorçana just next to the AB 197   district (see Figure 1.a for the location of the pumping station), and used exclusively for the irrigation of AB and being 198   its only resource. Flow measurements were made on a daily basis by the SAIH (Automatic Hydrological Information 199   System of the Ebro Basin; available at http://www.saihebro.com/saihebro/index.php; accessed 16 June 2023) and were 200   aggregated on a weekly basis to account for the time lag between pumping and actual irrigation (Olivera-Guerra et al., 201   2023). In addition, 5.8% of the pumped volume is removed to account for evaporative losses and leakage, based on a 202   comparison made in 2021 between the annual pumped water and annual irrigation measured with flowmeters at the district 203   level (Olivera-Guerra et al., 2023). In situ weekly irrigation data for the year 2019 are shown in Figure 1.b. [SOURCE: Page_104]

204   2.2.2 Field-scale in situ data [SOURCE: Page_104]

205   The instrumented fields Castello and Albesa are two double-cropped plots of 35 and 21 hectares respectively, located in 206   the AB district (see Figure 1.a for the location of the two instrumented fields). At Castello, SSM data every 15 minutes 207   are available for a five-month period in summer-fall 2021. At Albesa, SSM data every 15 minutes are available for three 208   periods: six months in summer-fall 2021, five months in winter-spring 2022, and five months in summer-fall 2022. For 209   Castello, SSM data are obtained from the average of SSM measurements of two TEROS 10 sensors (METER group) 210   installed at a depth of 5 cm and separated by about 100 m. For Albesa, they are derived from three sensors (two TEROS 211   10 and one EC-5; METER group) also about 100 m apart. For the periods mentioned, daily irrigation data from flowmeters 212   are available at both Castello and Albesa fields. These in situ data are used to test and evaluate the SSM-ASSIM approach 213   on a simple case (crop type and irrigation practices spatially uniform), at the plot scale, and with in situ SSM data being [SOURCE: Page_104]

6 [SOURCE: Page_104]

5.5. ARTICLE. RETRIEVING THE IRRIGATION ACTUALLY APPLIED AT DISTRICT SCALE : ASSIMILATING HIGH-RESOLUTION SENTINEL-1-DERIVED SOIL MOISTURE DATA INTO A FAO-56-BASED MODEL                                      93 [SOURCE: Page_105]

214   more frequent and less error prone than satellite observations. The in situ SSM measurements were averaged on a daily 215   basis and one day out of three was kept, resulting in an observation every three days. This provides a frequency higher 216   than that of S$_1$-derived SSM (the latter is six days), but low enough to mimic the frequency of satellite observations (2-3 217   days being the frequency of SMOS or SMAP). [SOURCE: Page_105]

218 219   2.2.3 In situ meteorological data [SOURCE: Page_105]

220   The meteorological data are obtained from five stations belonging to the Catalan meteorological station network (available 221   at https://ruralcat.gencat.cat/agrometeo.estacions; accessed 16 June 2023). Two of them are located within the AB district, 222   and three at a maximum distance of 5 km. The average standard deviation of both precipitation and ET$_0$ measurements 223   from the five stations is very low. Therefore, their spatial averages were used as forcing in the SAMIR model. [SOURCE: Page_105]

224 225   2.3 Remote sensing data [SOURCE: Page_105]

226   2.3.1 S$_2$-derived vegetation index [SOURCE: Page_105]

227   The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) is used in this study to drive the modeled crop development in 228   SAMIR. It is derived from the S$_2$ multispectral satellite constellation consisting of two satellites S2A and S2B, with a 229   global revisit frequency of five days. S2A and S2B were launched by the European Space Agency (ESA) in 2015 and 230   2017, respectively. We used the level 2 surface reflectance data at 10 m spatial resolution from band 4 (red) and band 8 231   (near-infrared) to compute NDVI, and cloud masks (QA60 and band 10) were applied. When more than 25% of the pixels 232   falling in a plot are affected by the cloud masks, all the pixels in that plot are removed to avoid cloud contamination. 233   When less than 25% of the plot is affected by the masks, the average of the remaining NDVI values within the crop field 234   is calculated. Finally, the field-scale NDVI data are interpolated to the daily scale using a piecewise cubic Hermite 235   interpolation polynomial method (Fritsch and Carlson, 1980). [SOURCE: Page_105]

236 237   2.3.2 S$_1$-derived SSM [SOURCE: Page_105]

238   The remotely sensed SSM data used in this study are derived from the S$_1$ C-band synthetic aperture radar satellite 239   constellation, consisting of two satellites S1A and S1B, with a global revisit frequency of six days. S1A and S1B were 240   launched by ESA in 2014 and 2016, respectively, and both provide dual acquisitions in VV (vertically transmitted, 241   vertically received) and VH (vertically transmitted, horizontally received) polarizations. To invert the SSM from S$_1$ 242   microwave observations, the approach proposed by Ouaadi et al. (2020) is used. The retrieval method is based on the 243   inversion of the water cloud model from the S$_1$ VV polarization backscattering coefficient and the S$_1$ interferometric 244   coherence. The vegetation descriptor used in the water cloud model is the above ground biomass derived from the 245   interferometric coherence. SSM is thus obtained at each S$_1$ acquisition and for each pixel by minimizing the distance 246   between the backscattering coefficient observed by S$_1$ and that simulated by the Water Cloud model, using a brute-force 247   approach. For more details on the S$_1$-derived SSM product, the reader is referred to the original paper by Ouaadi et al. 248   (2020). [SOURCE: Page_105]

7 [SOURCE: Page_105]

CHAPITRE 5. INVERSER L’IRRIGATION À PARTIR DE DONNÉES D’HUMIDITÉ DU 94                                                      SOL DE SURFACE [SOURCE: Page_106]

249   2.4 Ancillary soil data [SOURCE: Page_106]

250   The soil texture is relatively uniform over AB and corresponds to a silty clay soil (Jahn et al., 2006). It is derived from 251   the SoilGrids product (available at https://maps.isric.org; accessed 15 May 2023) at 250 m resolution (Hengl et al., 2017; 252   Poggio et al., 2021). Soil texture information is used in SAMIR to derive soil hydraulic properties, which control the 253   amount of water the soil can hold and the evaporation dynamics of the surface soil layer. [SOURCE: Page_106]

254 255   3 Method [SOURCE: Page_106]

256   The overall methodology for retrieving the weekly irrigation at the district scale is presented in the flowchart of Figure 2. 257   First, the SAMIR model is described with its irrigation module (3.1). Then, the SSM-ASSIM approach to retrieve the 258   daily irrigation parameters (SMthreshold and Idose) (3.2.1) and the strategy to simulate the weekly irrigation using the retrieved 259   SMthreshold and Idose as input parameters in SAMIR are presented (3.2.2). Finally, the strategy for applying the SSM-ASSIM 260   approach at the plot scale (section 3.3) and for evaluating irrigation retrievals at both field and district scale (section 3.4) 261   are described. [SOURCE: Page_106]

8 [SOURCE: Page_106]

5.5. ARTICLE. RETRIEVING THE IRRIGATION ACTUALLY APPLIED AT DISTRICT SCALE : ASSIMILATING HIGH-RESOLUTION SENTINEL-1-DERIVED SOIL MOISTURE DATA INTO A FAO-56-BASED MODEL                                      95 [SOURCE: Page_107]

262 263   Figure 2: Flowchart of the methodology to retrieve the weekly irrigation at district scale by assimilating SSM data into 264   the SAMIR model. [SOURCE: Page_107]

265 266   3.1 SAMIR model [SOURCE: Page_107]

267   SAMIR is a FAO-56 double-crop coefficient-based model (Allen et al., 1998) originally designed to simulate the crop 268   water balance components for estimating daily ET and optimal irrigation requirements, by considering the water status 269   of plant and soil. It uses meteorological forcing variables to calculate ET$_0$ (using the Penman-Monteith equation), 270   precipitation, crop and soil parameters, and NDVI to drive plant development. [SOURCE: Page_107]

9 [SOURCE: Page_107]

CHAPITRE 5. INVERSER L’IRRIGATION À PARTIR DE DONNÉES D’HUMIDITÉ DU 96                                                      SOL DE SURFACE [SOURCE: Page_108]

271   3.1.1 SAMIR main equations [SOURCE: Page_108]

272   SAMIR simulates the daily water balance equation as: [SOURCE: Page_108]

273   𝐷𝑟(𝑡) = 𝐷𝑟(𝑡 − 1) + 𝐸𝑇(𝑡) − 𝑃(𝑡) − 𝐼(𝑡) + 𝐷𝑃(𝑡)                                                           (1) [SOURCE: Page_108]

274   where Dr is the root zone depletion, ET the actual evapotranspiration, P the precipitation, I the irrigation and DP the deep 275   percolation. Each term is expressed in mm for day t (and t-1 for Dr) and ET is obtained by multiplying two crop 276   coefficients to ET$_0$ as follows: [SOURCE: Page_108]

277   𝐸𝑇(𝑡) = [𝐾𝑐𝑏(𝑡)・𝐾𝑠(𝑡) + 𝐾𝑒(𝑡)]・𝐸𝑇0 (𝑡)                                                                    (2) [SOURCE: Page_108]

278   where ET$_0$・Kcb・Ks is the water transpired by plants (T, mm), and ET$_0$・Ke the soil evaporation (E, mm). Kcb (-) is 279   the basal crop coefficient controlling potential crop transpiration, computed from a linear relationship with NDVI, Ks (-) 280   is the crop water stress coefficient reducing potential transpiration, and Ke (-) is the potential soil evaporation coefficient. [SOURCE: Page_108]

281   The calculation of Ks is based on the daily water balance calculation in the root zone layer, and can be written as: [SOURCE: Page_108]

282   𝐾𝑠(𝑡) = 𝑇𝐴𝑊(𝑡)−𝐷𝑟(𝑡) 𝑇𝐴𝑊(𝑡)・(1−𝑝) (3) [SOURCE: Page_108]

283   where Dr is calculated from the daily water balance according to Eq. (1), and TAW (mm) is the total (maximum) available 284   water in the root zone. p is a crop-specific parameter provided in the literature (Allen et al., 1998; Pereira et al., 2021), 285   ranging between 0.4 and 0.6 for most crops and being corrected daily for weather conditions. Allen et al. (1998) suggest 286   that p controls the water depth threshold below which irrigation should be triggered to avoid crop water stress (and irrigate 287   optimally) by keeping Dr below TAW・p. In other words, p triggers irrigation when soil moisture reaches a critical level 288   (below which the crop experiences water stress) called SMcritical, provided in the literature. p can then be written as follows: [SOURCE: Page_108]

289   𝑝 =1−( 𝑆𝑀𝑐𝑟𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑐𝑎𝑙 −𝑆𝑀𝑊𝑃 𝑆𝑀𝐹𝐶 −𝑆𝑀𝑊𝑃 )                                                                                   (4) [SOURCE: Page_108]

290   where SMFC (m^3 m-3) is the soil moisture at field capacity and SMWP (m^3 m-3) the soil moisture at wilting point, which are 291   both derived from soil texture using the pedotransfer function proposed by Román-Dobarco et al. (2019). In the AB 292   district, SMFC and SMWP derived from SoilGrids are fairly homogeneous with values of 0.330 (± 0.005) m^3 m-3 and 0.207 293   (± 0.006) m^3 m-3, respectively. For the Castello instrumented plot, SMFC and SMWP are 0.339 m^3 m-3 and 0.186 m^3 m-3, 294   respectively, and for Albesa 0.336 m^3 m-3 and 0.191 m^3 m-3. [SOURCE: Page_108]

295   Olivera-Guerra et al. (2023) proposed an alternative to the p parameter for triggering irrigation, called ptrigger. Unlike p, 296   ptrigger does not trigger irrigation when SMcritical is reached, but when SMthreshold is. SMthreshold is time-varying and can be 297   different from SMcritical, allowing to reproduce farmers' current practices. ptrigger is written as follows: [SOURCE: Page_108]

298   𝑝𝑡𝑟𝑖𝑔𝑔𝑒𝑟 (𝑡) = 1 − ( 𝑆𝑀𝑡ℎ𝑟𝑒𝑠ℎ𝑜𝑙𝑑 (𝑡)−𝑆𝑀𝑊𝑃 𝑆𝑀𝐹𝐶 −𝑆𝑀𝑊𝑃 )                                                                             (5) [SOURCE: Page_108]

299   TAW of Eq. (3) is computed as follows: [SOURCE: Page_108]

300   𝑇𝐴𝑊(𝑡) = (𝑆𝑀𝐹𝐶 − 𝑆𝑀𝑊𝑃 )・𝑍𝑟(𝑡)                                                                                               (6) [SOURCE: Page_108]

10 [SOURCE: Page_108]

313   3.1.2 Default irrigation simulation with SAMIR (FAO56-DEF approach) [SOURCE: Page_109]

314   SAMIR simulates irrigation using two irrigation parameters: SMthreshold and Idose. SMthreshold is the soil moisture level at 315   which irrigation is automatically triggered and is used to calculate ptrigger (see Eq. 5). Idose is the irrigation dose applied 316   when irrigation is triggered. By default, SAMIR uses SMthreshold and Idose values that produce a theoretically optimal 317   irrigation regime. We call this default irrigation mode FAO56-DEF. In the FAO56-DEF approach, irrigation is triggered 318   when SMthreshold equals SMcritical (see Eq. 5) and Idose is calculated as the amount of water required to completely fill the 319   root reservoir, without exceeding SMFC. With this approach, irrigation is triggered as soon as the simulated soil moisture 320   reaches SMcritical, thus avoiding crop water stress. Excess irrigation (generating drainage loss) is also avoided as Idose 321   fills the root reservoir up to the SMFC and not beyond. [SOURCE: Page_109]

322   3.1.3 Irrigation simulation in any irrigation regime with SAMIR [SOURCE: Page_109]

323   To represent real agricultural practices and associated irrigation regimes, Olivera-Guerra et al. (2023) proposed a time- 324   varying SMthreshold and Idose able to simulate actual irrigation. With time-varying values different from those used by 325   FAO56-DEF, it is possible to simulate time-varying irrigation water use in irrigation regime any (optimal, deficit or even 326   over). When SMthreshold is lower than SMcritical, this corresponds to a deficit irrigation regime, whereas when it is higher, it 327   corresponds to an over irrigation regime. Figure 3 illustrates for a theoretical double-cropped plot, the relative difference 328   between SMthreshold values for an ideal (SMthreshold set at SMcritical) and real (time-varying SMthreshold) case. The green line 329   represents the ideal case where irrigation is triggered at the onset of crop water stress (FAO56-DEF approach). The red 330   line represents the theoretical real case, with a variable SMthreshold (e.g., inverted from SSM data). We use herein the term 331   “real case” as opposed to “ideal case” here, but note that the variable SMthreshold in Figure 3 is theoretical and does not 332   correspond to a real experiment. In Figure 3, SMthreshold values below SMcritical in winter-spring would result in a deficit 333   irrigation regime (cf. red shaded area), as the theoretical irrigator waits for the soil moisture level to be low before [SOURCE: Page_109]

343   3.2 Retrieving irrigation from the assimilation of SSM observations (SSM-ASSIM) [SOURCE: Page_110]

344   3.2.1 Inverting the SMthreshold and Idose parameters [SOURCE: Page_110]

345   To retrieve the variable SMthreshold and Idose, SSM observations are assimilated into SAMIR using the PF method. The first 346   step of the PF method consists of randomly draw N initial samples (particles) with different parameter values. In our case, 347   300 particles with different (SMthreshold, Idose) pairs are generated following a uniform distribution between SMWP and 348   SMFC for SMthreshold, and between 0 and 20 mm d-1 for Idose. Next, simulations are performed for each particle and for each 349   day, until an observation is available (every six days for S$_1$-derived SSM, every three days for in situ SSM). On the day 350   of the SSM observation, the N simulated variables (here the 300 SSM simulated by SAMIR) are confronted with the 351   observation. During this evaluation step, each particle (SMthreshold and Idose pairs, resulting in SSM simulation) is assigned 352   a weight according to its likelihood with the observed SSM. The best particles are duplicated a number of times relative 353   to their likelihood, and the worst ones are discarded. [SOURCE: Page_110]

354   In order to calculate the weight of the particles, and also to prevent their degeneracy, the PF method takes into account 355   the model and observational errors. For the observed SSM errors, a standard deviation of 20% of the observed SSM value 356   is set for both S$_1$-derived SSM and in situ SSM, this value being in line with the errors of the existing SSM satellite 357   products (Das et al., 2019; Kerr et al., 2010). For the model error, a standard deviation of 10% of the parameter value is 358   applied to the three most sensitive SAMIR parameters (two parameters related to the NDVI-Kcb relationship and Zrmax; 359   Laluet et al., 2023a), as well as to the surface and root compartment depletions (De and Dr). To avoid particle degeneracy [SOURCE: Page_110]

5.5. ARTICLE. RETRIEVING THE IRRIGATION ACTUALLY APPLIED AT DISTRICT SCALE : ASSIMILATING HIGH-RESOLUTION SENTINEL-1-DERIVED SOIL MOISTURE DATA INTO A FAO-56-BASED MODEL                                      99 [SOURCE: Page_111]

360   as much as possible, their weights are reset whenever the effective sample size Neff reaches a threshold of one third of the 361   initial particle size number (for details see Moradkhani et al., 2005; van Leeuwen et al., 2019). [SOURCE: Page_111]

362   In addition, the 300 particles are reset to their initial values every 30 days, i.e.,, every five consecutive S$_1$-derived SSM 363   observations and ten in situ SSM observations. This results in monthly mean and standard deviation SMthreshold and Idose 364   values which are calculated using the particle weights obtained at the end of the month. The monthly timescale allows 365   accounting for changes in irrigation regime throughout the year, while ensuring a certain number of observations required 366   for the PF method to converge with satisfactory uncertainty. To obtain smoother SMthreshold and Idose values, the entire 367   assimilation scheme is then repeated five times, shifting the start date by six days each time. Subsequently, SMthreshold and 368   Idose are then obtained on a daily basis (mean and standard deviation) by averaging the five time series of monthly retrieved 369   SMthreshold and Idose. Figure 4 shows a flowchart describing the PF-based approach used in this study. [SOURCE: Page_111]

5.5. ARTICLE. RETRIEVING THE IRRIGATION ACTUALLY APPLIED AT DISTRICT SCALE : ASSIMILATING HIGH-RESOLUTION SENTINEL-1-DERIVED SOIL MOISTURE DATA INTO A FAO-56-BASED MODEL                                     101 [SOURCE: Page_113]

373   3.2.2 Simulating irrigation from the retrieved SMthreshold and Idose parameters [SOURCE: Page_113]

374   Once daily SMthreshold and Idose have been retrieved with the PF-based assimilation approach, they are used as input in 375   SAMIR to simulate irrigation. For this, 1000 time series of SMthreshold and Idose are randomly sampled following a normal 376   distribution with their retrieved daily mean and standard deviation, and are then used as input parameters in SAMIR to 377   simulate 1000 time series of daily irrigation. Daily irrigations are then aggregated at the weekly scale, and the mean and 378   standard deviation of weekly irrigation are obtained from the 1000 simulated weekly irrigation time series. [SOURCE: Page_113]

379 [SOURCE: Page_113]

380   3.3 Aggregation at the crop type scale [SOURCE: Page_113]

381   To simplify our approach as much as possible, and to minimize its computational cost, we selected the five main crop 382   types (double crops, summer cereals, winter cereals, forages, and fruit trees) representing 94% of the irrigated area in 383   2019, and computed the average of their inputs (NDVI, SSM, and soil texture) weighted by their total surface area. This 384   results in five average plots representing 94 % of the irrigated part of AB. The remaining 6% is represented by the average 385   of the five main crop types. Averaging the plots by crop type is justified by the fact that the soil texture is fairly 386   homogeneous over the area (in addition to having a low sensitivity in SAMIR; Laluet et al., 2023a). Figure 5 shows the 387   mean and standard deviation of the S$_1$-derived SSM and the S$_2$-derived NDVI time series for the five average plots. The 388   dynamics of NDVI and SSM time series observed for plots belonging to a given crop type are not strongly scattered 389   (Figure 5) reflecting homogeneity in terms of farming practices (sowing date, irrigation practices). At the end of the SSM- 390   ASSIM process, the simulated irrigations for each of the five average plots are averaged and weighted by their total area 391   within AB to obtain an irrigation amount representative of the entire AB district. [SOURCE: Page_113]

393   Figure 5: Mean and standard deviation of S$_1$-derived SSM (left) and S$_2$-derived NDVI (right) for each of the five main 394   crop types for 2019. [SOURCE: Page_114]

395 396   3.4 Evaluation of retrieved irrigation [SOURCE: Page_114]

397   The Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD), the Pearson correlation coefficient (r) and the bias between retrieved and in 398   situ weekly irrigation are calculated. At the district scale, this is done for both SSM-ASSIM and FAO56-DEF approaches, 399   and the uncertainty simulated with SSM-ASSIM is assessed. At the plot scale, only SSM-ASSIM is evaluated. [SOURCE: Page_114]

400 401 402   4 Results and discussion [SOURCE: Page_114]

403   In this section, we first present the irrigation results obtained by applying the SSM-ASSIM approach at the scale of the 404   Albesa and Castello plots, using in situ SSM data every three days for assimilation (Section 4.1). Then, the irrigation 405   results obtained with the SSM-ASSIM and FAO56-DEF approaches at the district scale using S$_1$-derived SSM data are 406   presented and discussed (4.2.1). Finally, the results of the SSM-ASSIM approach are put into perspective with other work 407   (4.2.2) and limitations and perspectives are highlighted (4.2.3). [SOURCE: Page_114]

408 [SOURCE: Page_114]

409   4.1 Field-scale experiment using in situ SSM [SOURCE: Page_114]

410   This section aims to assess the performance of SSM-ASSIM at the field scale where the crop type and irrigation practices 411   can be considered spatially uniform. In situ SSM data from the double-cropped fields Albesa and Castello are used. Figure 412   6 shows the results for the two plots and the four periods studied: Castello summer-fall 2021 (a), Albesa summer-fall 413   2021 (b), Albesa winter-spring 2022 (c), and Albesa summer-fall 2022 (d). Each plot shows, in addition to rainfall, the in 414   situ SSM (purple line), the SMthreshold (dark blue line) and the Idose (light blue line) retrieved with SSM-ASSIM, and the 415   simulated irrigation using the retrieved SMthreshold and Idose as forcing in SAMIR (green line) along with the observed 416   irrigation (black line). Standard deviation of the input SSM data set (used for assimilation; 20% of the observed value), 417   SMthreshold, Idose and simulated irrigation are shown. Bias and RMSD values are given in the chart titles. Note that no bias 418   correction between simulated and observed SSM was applied. [SOURCE: Page_114]

CHAPITRE 5. INVERSER L’IRRIGATION À PARTIR DE DONNÉES D’HUMIDITÉ DU 104                                                     SOL DE SURFACE [SOURCE: Page_116]

425   Figure 6 should be read as follows: the assimilation of in situ SSM data in SAMIR results in a daily SMthreshold and a daily 426   Idose which, given as forcing to SAMIR, provides the irrigation retrieved by the SSM-ASSIM approach. For example, in 427   Figure 6.b we can observe that the relatively low in situ SSM values at the beginning of the season (about 0.20 m^3 m-3) 428   suddenly increase to about 0.28 m^3 m-3 when the irrigation season starts. This results in a retrieved SMthreshold that rapidly 429   increases from 0.23 to 0.27 m^3 m-3, and an Idose that rises from about 10 mm d-1 to over 15 mm d-1 when the irrigation 430   season begins. By using these SMthreshold and Idose pairs as forcing in SAMIR, the simulated irrigation reproduces pretty 431   well the start of the irrigation season. [SOURCE: Page_116]

432   Figure 6 shows that our approach correctly reproduces the irrigation start and end dates for each season. It also indicates 433   that SSM-ASSIM slightly overestimates irrigation during the winter-spring season (mostly in June; Figure 6.c), while 434   underestimating it during the three summer-fall seasons (Figures 6.a, 6.b, and 6.d). This results in a bias of +4.6 mm week- 435   1 for Albesa winter-spring 2022, -2.3 mm week-1 for Castello summer-fall 2021, -5.4 mm week-1 for Albesa summer-fall 436   2021, and -9.4 mm week-1 for Albesa summer-fall 2022. The RMSD for Albesa winter-spring 2022 is 9.3 mm week-1, 437   while it is slightly larger for Castello summer-fall 2021 (12.2 mm week-1), Albesa summer-fall 2021 (14.6 mm week-1) 438   and Albesa summer-fall 2022 (14.7 mm week-1). Note that the irrigation amounts are much higher during summer-fall 439   (between 40 and 70 mm week-1 for the most intensive irrigation period in August-September) than during the winter- 440   spring season (between 0 and 40 mm week-1), hence explaining the higher RMSD values obtained in summer-fall. [SOURCE: Page_116]

441   For the three summer-fall seasons, SSM-ASSIM generally underestimates irrigation (-12% for Castello summer-fall 2021, 442   -20% for Albesa summer-fall 2021, and -32% for Albesa summer-fall 2022). For these three seasons, simulated weekly 443   irrigation never exceeds 50 mm week-1. During the most intensive irrigation period, simulated weekly irrigation is 444   generally between 25 and 40 mm week-1, while the observed irrigation is between 40 and 60 mm week-1. This means that 445   the weekly simulated irrigation, although too low, is sufficient for the simulated SSM to match the observed SSM. Indeed, 446   SMthreshold and Idose are inverted from the observed SSM. Therefore, if more irrigation would have been needed to better 447   match the simulated and observed SSM, the inverted SMthreshold would have been larger during the intensive irrigation 448   seasons (to trigger more frequent irrigation events), as well as the inverted Idose (to irrigate with a larger amount of 449   water). We hypothesize that one of the reasons for this is the nonlinearity in the relationship between SSM and irrigation. 450   Let’s consider a farmer who irrigate a field heavily with sprinklers (e.g., 10 mm d-1). During the first hour of irrigation, 451   the SSM can vary rapidly from low (dry soil) to high values (wet soil). As the irrigation event continues, the water applied 452   will generate a weaker response in terms of SSM variation than at the start of irrigation, due in particular to infiltration 453   into the underlying soil layer. This is illustrated in Figure 6, where we can see that the underestimation in summer 454   generally occurs when the in situ SSM is at high values, close to SMFC (~0.34 m^3 m-3). [SOURCE: Page_116]

455 [SOURCE: Page_116]

457   4.2.1 Evaluation of the SSM-ASSIM and FAO56-DEF approaches [SOURCE: Page_116]

458   Figure 7 shows the retrieved weekly irrigation at AB in 2019 with SSM-ASSIM (green line) and FAO56-DEF (orange 459   line), together with in situ irrigation data (black line). SSM-ASSIM reproduces the beginning and end of irrigation season 460   and the general irrigation dynamics quite well (RMSD of 6.7 mm week-1 and r of 0.88; Table 1). In contrast, FAO56-DEF 461   does not reproduce the observed irrigation dynamics (RMSD of 16.7 mm week-1, and r of 0.47), as it simulates few 462   irrigation events with large doses. In terms of bias over the whole year 2019, SSM-ASSIM (+0.3 mm week-1) is slightly [SOURCE: Page_116]

474   In line with the results for the field-scale experiment using in situ data (Section 4.1), SSM-ASSIM underestimates 475   irrigation for the summer-fall period (bias of -2.6 mm week-1). However, the underestimation in summer is less 476   pronounced at the district scale than at the field scale (Albesa summer-fall 2021 has a bias of -5.4 mm week-1 and Albesa 477   summer-fall 2021 of -9.4 mm week-1). In contrast to the latter, at the AB district scale, SSM-ASSIM is able to simulate 478   summer irrigation values close to the observed maxima (41 mm week-1 simulated in mid-August 2019, for an in situ 479   irrigation of 46 mm week-1; cf. Figure 7). This may be due to the lower values of observed irrigation during the intensive 480   summer irrigation period at the AB scale (around 40 mm week-1), where there are different types of crops, compared to 481   the Albesa and Castello fields (around 50 to 60 mm week-1), where there is only maize. Consequently, the limitation 482   mentioned in Section 4.1 regarding the difficulty of simulating high weekly irrigation amounts, even with high observed 483   SSM values, is less of a problem at the AB scale. This suggests that the SSM-ASSIM approach is particularly suited to 484   the district scale: different crop types with different irrigation regimes are considered together at the district scale, and the 485   weighted (by crop type) average of the observed irrigation in summer is lower than on highly irrigated (100 % maize) 486   plots such as Albesa and Castello. [SOURCE: Page_118]

487   SSM-ASSIM tends to overestimate irrigation during the winter-spring season (bias of +3.7 mm week-1), consistent with 488   the field scale results (Section 4.1). While irrigation amounts and dynamics are well reproduced for the months of January 489   to April, an overestimation occurs in May-June. To understand why, Figure 8 shows the time series of precipitation (a), 490   S$_1$-derived SSM (b), as well as the retrieved SMthreshold (c), Idose (d), and irrigation (e) with SSM-ASSIM for the main crop 491   type (double crop) in the area. From May to mid-June 2019, S$_1$-derived SSM detects irrigation, with the SSM increasing 492   from 0.11 m^3 m-3 at the beginning of May to 0.28 m^3 m-3 at the end of May. This large difference in SSM generates a 493   significant increase in both retrieved SMthreshold and Idose, leading to important weekly irrigation in May for the double- 494   cropped plots, which in turn led to an overestimation of irrigation at the AB scale at that time. In fact, the moments of 495   strong SSM growth correspond to those when simulated irrigation is largest. Furthermore, although the average weekly 496   irrigation simulated with SSM-ASSIM for all AB performs satisfactorily, the associated uncertainty is significant (±53%, 497   706 ± 375 mm year-1; shaded green area in Figure 7). [SOURCE: Page_118]

504   This section aims to put the results obtained with SSM-ASSIM into perspective by comparing them with other results 505   obtained for the same irrigation district using a different approach. The latter is that proposed by Dari et al. (2023), which, 506   to our knowledge, is the only work to date that has dealt with the estimation of irrigation from satellite-based SSM data 507   on the AB district for the year 2019 (their study covers the years 2016 to 2019). (2023) provided that the weekly irrigation they simulated at the 1 km pixel scale for several irrigation 509   districts, including AB (https://zenodo.org/record/7341284; accessed 20 June 2023). [SOURCE: Page_119]

510   Dari et al. (2023) used an approach based on the SM2RAIN algorithm described in the introduction (Section 1), which 511   differs significantly from SSM-ASSIM, in particular because of its simpler formalism which relies heavily on observed 512   SSM data and empirical parameters that require calibration. CHAPITRE 5. INVERSER L’IRRIGATION À PARTIR DE DONNÉES D’HUMIDITÉ DU 108                                                     SOL DE SURFACE [SOURCE: Page_120]

513   use is 1 km, as are the irrigation simulations. In contrast, our approach is based on a finer scale simulation of crop water 514   consumption, taking into account model and observational errors. Furthermore, SSM-ASSIM uses an S$_1$-derived SSM 515   product with a resolution of 15 m. [SOURCE: Page_120]

516   Another point distinguishes the two approaches. SSM-ASSIM simulates only the plots in AB that were actually irrigated 517   during the study year, representing 61.4 km² in 2019. On the other hand, Dari et al. (2023) simulated all AB plots equipped 518   for irrigation, regardless of whether or not they were actually irrigated during the study year, i.e., 70.9 km². In this section, 519   in order to compare the results obtained with the two approaches, the irrigation (in mm) simulated with SSM-ASSIM 520   (and in situ) were adjusted to represent the irrigation applied on the 70.9 km², consistent with the irrigation simulated by 521   Dari et al. (2023). In addition, Dari et al. (2023) removed 10% of the in situ irrigation data to account for losses, while 522   only 5.8% was removed in this study as explained in Section 2.2.1. [SOURCE: Page_120]

523   Figure 9 shows for the year 2019 the weekly irrigation obtained with SM2RAIN (red line), the one obtained with SSM- 524   ASSIM (green line), and the in situ irrigation (black line). Although both approaches are able to capture the irrigation 525   signal, SM2RAIN underperforms SSM-ASSIM, with a more pronounced underestimation of irrigation and an RMSD of 526   9.7 mm week-1 (6.7 mm week-1 for SSM-ASSIM), a bias of -3.3 mm week-1 (+0.3 mm week-1), and an r of 0.65 (and 0.88) 527   for the year 2019 (Table 2). While SM2RAIN manages to reproduce relatively well the dynamics at the start of the 2019 528   summer-fall irrigation season in July, it significantly underestimates irrigation during the months of August and 529   September, when irrigation is particularly intense (Figure 9). [SOURCE: Page_120]

5.5. ARTICLE. RETRIEVING THE IRRIGATION ACTUALLY APPLIED AT DISTRICT SCALE : ASSIMILATING HIGH-RESOLUTION SENTINEL-1-DERIVED SOIL MOISTURE DATA INTO A FAO-56-BASED MODEL                                     109 [SOURCE: Page_121]

535   Figure 9: Top: daily rainfall in AB. Bottom: weekly irrigation simulated at the AB scale with the SM2RAIN approach 536   (Dari et al., 2023) (red line), with the SSM-ASSIM approach (green line), and observed irrigation (black line), for 2019. [SOURCE: Page_121]

537 538   Such differences in terms of performance may be a consequence of certain features of the SSM-ASSIM approach. In 539   particular, we believe that the implementation of the approach at the plot scale, which allows to capture the plot-level 540   processes governing crop consumption, is key to simulating irrigation dynamics. This plot-scale approach is made 541   possible by the quality and the fine spatial resolution of the S$_1$-derived SSM product used in this study, which provides a 542   distinct SSM signature for each plot and thus an irrigation signature for each plot. [SOURCE: Page_121]

543 [SOURCE: Page_121]

544   4.2.3 Quality of S$_1$-derived SSM product and its impact on the SSM-ASSIM irrigation retrieval [SOURCE: Page_121]

545   Figure 7 shows that most of the irrigation underestimation with the SSM-ASSIM approach using S$_1$-derived SSM occurs 546   in July (at the beginning of the summer-fall irrigation season). We believe that these underestimates are related to the 547   difficulty of the S$_1$-derived SSM product in detecting the actual SSM at the beginning of the second irrigation season 548   (when vegetation is poorly developed) for double-cropped fields. [SOURCE: Page_121]

549   This assumption is supported by two elements: [SOURCE: Page_121]

550       1) Figure 8.b shows low S$_1$-derived SSM values for double-cropped plots in late June and early July, at the 551            beginning of the summer-fall irrigation season. However, in situ irrigation at the AB scale (black line in Figure 552            7) shows that the summer irrigation season has already started by then. There is a difference of about one month 553            between the start of the summer-fall irrigation season at the AB scale and the increase in S$_1$-derived SSM for 554            the double-cropped plots. However, we would expect the reanalyzed SSM to increase more rapidly after the start 555            of the irrigation season, since the double-cropped plots represent 62% of the irrigated AB area. [SOURCE: Page_121]

556       2) At the plot level, the time lag between the first irrigation events of the second growing season and the first 557            significant increase in S$_1$-derived SSM is also observed. Figure 10.a shows rainfall (black bar) and in situ 558            irrigation (orange area) for the summer-fall 2021 season at the Albesa instrumented plot. Figure 10.b shows the 559            daily in situ SSM (red line) and the S$_1$-derived SSM (blue line) for the same plot. Note that the in situ and S$_1$- 560            derived SSMs have been normalized between their minimum and maximum values to facilitate their comparison. 561            It appears that when the irrigation season starts at the end of June, in situ SSM increases almost immediately, 562            while the S$_1$-derived SSM starts to increase a month later, around the end of July. [SOURCE: Page_121]

CHAPITRE 5. INVERSER L’IRRIGATION À PARTIR DE DONNÉES D’HUMIDITÉ DU 110                                                     SOL DE SURFACE [SOURCE: Page_122]

563 [SOURCE: Page_122]

564   Figure 10: For the Albesa (21 hectares) double crop plot: daily in situ rain (black bars) and irrigation (orange line) (a), 565   daily in situ SSM (red line) and S$_1$-derived SSM every six days (blue line) normalized between their minimum and 566   maximum values (b), for the period from June 2021 to November 2021. [SOURCE: Page_122]

567 [SOURCE: Page_122]

568   Figure A$_1$ was added to the Appendix to explain why low S$_1$-derived SSM values are observed over the double-cropped 569   plots at the beginning of the summer season. Figure A$_1$ shows time series of S$_1$ backscattering coefficient, S$_1$-derived 570   interferometric coherence (used as vegetation descriptor), S$_1$-derived SSM and S$_2$-derived NDVI (related to vegetation 571   development) over the Albesa field for 2019. During the intercrop period in early summer, the maximum coherence is 572   0.6 while in winter it is above 0.7 (as in Ouaadi et al., 2021; Santoro et al., 2010). This low level of interferometric 573   coherence in early summer indicates that the scatterer structure is different between the winter and summer inter-seasons. 574   This is probably due to the fact that in AB maize is directly sown without tillage in summer, leaving the soil partially 575   covered by the remaining stalks, unlike in winter. However, the relationship between coherence and above-ground 576   biomass used in the inversion process is calibrated assuming that the growing season begins with bare soil (and therefore 577   with a coherence value assumed to be greater than 0.7). With a coherence of 0.6 observed in AB during early summer, a 578   bias appears in the SSM retrieved at that time. This is explained by the fact that the radiative transfer model used for the 579   inversion process reaches the observed level of backscatter with the contribution of the canopy only with dry soil 580   underneath. Furthermore, this phenomenon seems to occur only in the case of double-cropped plots; other crop types with 581   a single crop per year (winter cereals and summer cereals) don't seem to be affected by this problem. [SOURCE: Page_122]

582   Identifying this difficulty in detecting SSM in early summer (when two crops are grown consecutively in the same year) 583   in the SSM inversion algorithm proposed by Ouaadi et al. (2020) represents an important avenue for improving the quality 584   of S$_1$-derived SSM on double crop fields, and consequently the performance of the SSM-ASSIM approach. With a higher 585   S$_1$-derived SSM value at the beginning of the summer irrigation season, more irrigation would be retrieved by SSM- 586   ASSIM, thus reducing the summer underestimation issue, and improving the assimilation performance. [SOURCE: Page_122]

5.5. ARTICLE. RETRIEVING THE IRRIGATION ACTUALLY APPLIED AT DISTRICT SCALE : ASSIMILATING HIGH-RESOLUTION SENTINEL-1-DERIVED SOIL MOISTURE DATA INTO A FAO-56-BASED MODEL                                     111 [SOURCE: Page_123]

588   5 Summary and conclusion [SOURCE: Page_123]

589   With increasing pressure on water resources, managers and decision makers need to know how much water is being used 590   for irrigation. However, there is a lack of reliable information on these quantities at all spatial scales. To address this need, 591   a growing number of studies have proposed approaches combining models and satellite observations, in particular SSM. 592   Although encouraging results have been obtained, state-of-the-art SSM-based irrigation retrieval methods have been 593   limited by the spatio-temporal resolution of available SSM data, and the difficulty of representing irrigation-related 594   processes over large areas and to explicitly account for uncertainties in irrigation estimates. [SOURCE: Page_123]

595   To fill this gap, we propose a new approach (SSM-ASSIM) to assimilate high spatial resolution (15 m) SSM data into the 596   FAO-56-based SAMIR model at the plot scale using a PF assimilation method that address the above-mentioned 597   challenges. The output of SSM-ASSIM is the mean and standard deviation of two smoothed monthly parameters of the 598   SAMIR irrigation module, namely SMthreshold and Idose, which control the irrigation trigger and dose, respectively. 599   The retrieved irrigation and its uncertainty are obtained at weekly scale by running SAMIR with the retrieved distribution 600   of SMthreshold and Idose as forcing. For validation, the approach is applied to two instrumented fields for which in situ 601   SSM and irrigation data are available, and to the 8000 ha AB irrigation district for which in situ irrigation data are 602   available. At the district scale, irrigation is also simulated with the FAO-56 default configuration (FAO56-DEF) as a 603   benchmark to assess the performance of SSM-ASSIM. [SOURCE: Page_123]

604   Results at the plot scale using in situ SSM data show that SSM-ASSIM reproduces the irrigation dynamics very well 605   throughout the agricultural season. However, an underestimation occurs during periods of intense irrigation for the three 606   summer-fall seasons. This can be explained by the large amounts of irrigation applied to these plots in summer, which 607   are not fully captured in the SSM signal as they exceed ~50 mm week-1. A slight overestimation is also observed for the 608   winter-spring season. When applied at the district scale using S$_1$-derived SSM data, SSM-ASSIM clearly outperforms 609   FAO56-DEF and can reproduce the observed weekly irrigation quite well, with an r of 0.88 and an RMSD of 6.7 mm 610   week-1 for the year 2019. However, as with the field-scale experiments, SSM-ASSIM tends to overestimate irrigation in 611   winter-spring (bias of +3.7 mm week-1) and underestimate it in summer-fall (-2.6 mm week-1). The overestimation in 612   winter-spring is related to the discrepancy between very low SSM values at the start of the season, followed by a sudden 613   increase in SSM (observed for the double-cropped plots representing 62% of the AB area), resulting in high levels of 614   simulated irrigation. The underestimation in summer is attributed to the degraded quality of the S$_1$-derived SSM in early 615   summer for the double-cropped plots. [SOURCE: Page_123]

616   The performance of SSM-ASSIM depends on the quality of the SSM product. Therefore, any improvement in the accuracy 617   and precision of field-scale SSM estimates would improve the quality of irrigation retrievals. In addition, the relationship 618   between SSM and irrigation is highly non-linear due to the shallow depth (~0-5 cm) sensed by microwave sensors. 619   Saturation of SSM sensitivity to large amounts of irrigation is an intrinsic limitation of SSM-based assimilation 620   approaches. This problem could eventually be solved by the joint assimilation of thermal-derived ET data, which, in 621   hydric stress conditions are directly linked to the soil moisture accumulated in the root zone. This prospect is all the more 622   encouraging as new thermal missions will soon be launched with Land Surface Temperature Monitoring (LSTM; Koetz 623   et al., 2018) and Thermal infraRed Imaging Satellite for High-resolution Natural resource Assessment (TRISHNA; 624   Lagouarde et al., 2018), which will provide ET and crop stress index products with unprecedented high spatial and 625   temporal resolution in the near-future. Finally, the SSM-ASSIM approach could be integrated into large scale LSM to 626   take more realistically account for irrigation and its impact on the hydrological cycle. [SOURCE: Page_123]

CHAPITRE 5. INVERSER L’IRRIGATION À PARTIR DE DONNÉES D’HUMIDITÉ DU 120                                                     SOL DE SURFACE [SOURCE: Page_132]

5.6    Conclusion, limites, et perspectives L’approche SSM-ASSIM affiche des résultats encourageants avec une bonne capacité à repro- duire la dynamique de l’irrigation hebdomadaire observée, que ce soit à l’échelle des parcelles instrumentées Albesa et Castello (en utilisant des données de SSM in situ) ou du périmètre irri- gué d’AB (en utilisant des données de SSM dérivées de S$_1$). Sa force principale réside dans le fait d’assimiler des données de SSM à haute résolution spatiale permettant de détecter efficacement la signature de l’irrigation, et de les assimiler dans un modèle simulant de manière robuste le bilan d’eau des cultures à l’échelle de la parcelle. [SOURCE: Page_132]

Quelques limites sont cependant à mentionner, menant à des interrogations qui peuvent ouvrir à des perspectives intéressantes d’investigations futures. J’en dresse une brève liste ci-dessous, mais ces limites et perspectives sont approfondies dans le Chapitre 7. - SSM-ASSIM a été appliquée et évaluée à l’échelle du périmètre irrigué sur une seule année hydrologique (2019). Est-ce que sur d’autres années hydrologiques les résultats obtenus à cette échelle auraient été meilleurs ? Moins bons ? Pourquoi ? - SSM-ASSIM a été appliqué sur seulement deux parcelles et un périmètre irrigué. Est-ce que sur d’autres parcelles, et sur d’autres périmètres irrigués les résultats obtenus auraient été meilleurs ? Moins bons ? Pourquoi ? - Ces exercices de validation supplémentaires permettraient en outre de mieux comprendre l’approche, et notamment de mieux expliquer la surestimation observée fin avril à l’échelle du périmètre. Cette surestimation est-elle liée à la qualité du produit de SSM ou au for- malisme de notre approche ? - Le travail présenté a souligné la difficulté de SSM-ASSIM à reproduire les quantités d’ir- rigation hebdomadaires en été, lorsque ces dernières sont très importantes. Cette difficulté pourrait-elle être surmontée en améliorant le formalisme de SAMIR ? - Pour mieux contraindre les paramètres SMthreshold et Idose , il serait possible d’assimiler, conjointement aux données de SSM, des produits d’ET à haute résolution. En effet, l’ET contient une information sur l’humidité du sol de la zone racinaire (bien que limitée à la transpiration maximale des plantes) qui est clé dans la modélisation du bilan d’eau. [SOURCE: Page_132]

6.1    Introduction Nous l’avons vu, le suivi du drainage des zones irriguées est clé pour les gestionnaires car il est important de trouver un équilibre entre un drainage minimum pour éviter la salinisation des sols en lessivant les sels qui s’y accumulent (dans le cas des sols salins), et un drainage trop important pour éviter de nuire à la qualité des cours d’eau situés à l’aval (les eaux de drainage étant chargées en nutriments et/ou en sel et/ou en pesticides) et pour limiter les pertes d’eau. La plupart des modèles de simulation du drainage existants sont à base physique (par exemple, HYDRUS-2D, ADAPT, RZ2SQM, DRAINMOD) et sont composés de nombreux paramètres, nécessitant 1) de travailler sur des sites pour lesquels de nombreuses données in situ existent afin de renseigner les valeurs des paramètres (lorsque des mesures in situ sont réalisables), et 2) une opération de calibration pouvant être lourde (lorsque les mesures in situ ne sont pas ou difficilement réalisables). Cela rend difficilement envisageable une utilisation spatialisée de ces modèles sur des sites ne disposant pas nécessairement de nombreuses données in situ. Dans ce contexte ce chapitre vise à évaluer les performances de quatre modèles parcimonieux de simulation du drainage, en utilisant les données de drainage des sous-bassins AB$_1$ et AB$_2$ présentés dans le Chapitre 2, d’abord en les calibrant avec des données de drainage (évaluation de la précision), puis en utilisant des valeurs de paramètres par défaut issues de la littérature pour les calibrer (évaluation de l’exactitude, accuracy). [SOURCE: Page_133]

## 122                CHAPITRE 6. SIMULER LE DRAINAGE DES PÉRIMÈTRES IRRIGUÉS

6.2    Les quatre modèles de drainage Les modèles évalués sont construits à partir d’une combinaison de deux modèles de surface (RU et SAMIR) permettant de simuler la recharge, et de deux modèles souterrains (Reservoir et SIDRA) convertissant la recharge en débit de drainage aux exutoires à la sortie des sous-bassins. Ils forment alors quatre modèles : RU-Reservoir, SAMIR-Reservoir, RU-SIDRA, SAMIR-SIDRA. - RU (Henine et al., 2022; Jeantet et al., 2021) ne compte qu’un seul paramètre principal (qui intègre l’essentiel de la sensibilité), Sinter (mm), qui régit la taille du réservoir de sol ainsi le moment où le drainage débute (lorsque le réservoir de sol est plein). - SIDRA (Lesaffre and Zimmer, 1987; Bouarfa and Zimmer, 2000) est un modèle à base physique résolvant l’équation de Boussinesq et comptant deux paramètres principaux. - Reservoir (Cenobio-Cruz et al., 2023) simule une vidange exponentielle d’un réservoir rempli par la recharge, suivant l’équation Q(t) = Z(t) · k, avec Z (mm) le niveau d’eau dans le réservoir théorique, et k (-) un coefficient de déplétion étant généralement inférieur à 0.1. Alors que les principales caractéristiques des quatre modèles sont décrites dans la Table 6.1, une description détaillée de ces derniers se trouve dans l’article présenté Section 6.5. [SOURCE: Page_134]

## 6.3. ÉVALUATION DE LA PRÉCISION DES MODÈLES                                                          123

différents degrés de complexité) peuvent-ils reproduire le drainage observé en étant calibré avec des données de drainage ?”. [SOURCE: Page_135]

6.3.1   Méthode de calibration La méthode de calibration utilisée se nomme Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm (NSGA-II ; Deb et al. 2002) et fait partie de la famille des algorithmes évolutionnistes qui sont largement utilisés dans diverses disciplines pour leurs performances élevées. La méthode NSGA- II a été utilisée dans ce travail car elle est efficace en termes de coût computationnel, et qu’elle permet d’optimiser plusieurs fonctions objectifs à la fois (calibration multi-objectifs). Cela est très utile car les modèles utilisant SAMIR ont besoin de calibrer deux fonctions objectifs : l’une pour le drainage et l’autre pour l’irrigation. En effet, SAMIR étant utilisé de manière spatialisée à l’échelle de parcelle, cela implique que l’irrigation qu’il utilise soit spatialisée également. Or, la seule donnée d’irrigation disponible au périmètre d’AB est celle issue de la station de pompage, qui n’est pas spatialisée. Pour spatialiser cette dernière, les valeurs de SMthreshold et de Idose inversées pour le périmètre d’AB en 2019 et correspondant à une irrigation réaliste (en assimilant les données d’irrigation, voir Chapitre 4), ont été appliquées à chaque parcelle du périmètre d’AB modélisée par SAMIR. L’irrigation est ainsi simulée au niveau de chaque parcelle avec des valeurs de SMthreshold et de Idose correspondant à des pratiques réalistes. Lorsque l’irrigation de chaque parcelle du périmètre d’AB est agrégée, l’irrigation obtenue est semblable à celle mesurée à la station de pompage (Olivera-Guerra et al., 2023). Cependant, en modifiant les paramètres sensibles de SAMIR pour calibrer le drainage simulé, l’irrigation simulée risque d’être modifiée, et de s’éloigner de celle qui a été réellement appliquée sur le périmètre. C’est précisément pour éviter cela qu’une calibration multi-objectifs est utilisée ici : elle permet de calibrer le drainage et l’irrigation à la fois, afin de s’assurer que l’ajustement des paramètres pour simuler le drainage n’entraı̂ne pas une dégradation trop importante de l’irrigation simulée. Une règle a alors été fixée : la meilleure simulation du drainage, ayant la fonction objectif KGE (Q ) la plus élevée (voir l’article présenté Section 6.5 pour plus d’information sur KGE (Q$_0$.5 )), 0.5 [SOURCE: Page_135]

est choisie, à condition que le RMSD de l’irrigation simulée (agrégée à l’échelle du périmètre et évaluée avec les données d’irrigation pompée) correspondant soit inférieur à 0.7 mm/jour (valeur de RMSD correspondant à celles obtenues au maximum dans le Chapitre 4 lors de l’évaluation de la simulation réaliste de l’irrigation). [SOURCE: Page_135]

La Figure 6.1 montre comment l’algorithme NSGA-II ajuste les trois principaux paramètres du modèle SAMIR-Reservoir (aKcb , Zrmax , k) en fonction du nombre de simulations réalisées. NSGA-II ajuste simulation après simulation les jeux de paramètres qui permettent de réaliser les meilleures simulations de drainage et d’irrigation (étant les plus proches du drainage observé et de l’irrigation observée). Une description plus approfondie de la méthode NSGA-II est à retrouver dans l’article présenté Section 6.5. [SOURCE: Page_135]

6.3.2   Résultats Les résultats du drainage simulé par les quatre modèles en les calibrant sur les données de drainage du sous-bassin AB$_2$ pour les deux périodes analysées (2021 et 2022) sont présentés Figure 6.2, avec les valeurs de KGE (Q$_0$.5 ) obtenues. Les résultats pour le sous-bassin AB$_1$ sont présentés dans l’article de la Section 6.5. [SOURCE: Page_135]

Sur les deux sous-bassins AB$_1$ et AB$_2$, RU-Reservoir est le plus précis (KGE (Q$_0$.5 ) moyen de 0.87), suivi de SAMIR-Reservoir (0.79), RU-SIDRA (0.76), et SAMIR-SIDRA (0.68). Ces [SOURCE: Page_135]

## 124               CHAPITRE 6. SIMULER LE DRAINAGE DES PÉRIMÈTRES IRRIGUÉS

Figure 6.1 – Évolution des trois paramètres principaux du modèle SAMIR-Reservoir en fonction du nombre de simulations réalisées avec l’algorithme de calibration NSGA-II. [SOURCE: Page_136]

différences en termes de performances s’expliquent par deux facteurs. Premièrement, et c’est le facteur le plus important, le formalisme du modèle souterrain Re- servoir est plus adapté que celui de SIDRA à la faible réactivité du drainage observée à AB$_1$ et AB$_2$. Le drainage observé sur ces sous-bassins est caractérisé par une faible dynamique, no- tamment du fait que toutes les parcelles ne sont pas équipées de drain. Dans le cas des parcelles non équipées de drains, l’excès d’eau d’irrigation ou de pluie s’infiltrant sous les racines met plus de temps à être transporté jusqu’aux collecteurs. Le modèle SIDRA a été développé et évalué sur des sous-bassins totalement équipés de drains, et ayant donc une réactivité plus importante que les sous-bassins AB$_1$ et AB$_2$. SIDRA est bien adapté pour simuler des pics importants de débit de drainage suivis de décroissances rapides (Jeantet et al., 2021; Henine et al., 2022). Le modèle Reservoir au contraire consiste en une seule équation permettant de simuler les écoule- ments faibles (low flows, par opposition aux écoulements rapides provenant du ruissellement) ; il n’a pas de terme dans son formalisme permettant de simuler des pics importants de débits. Deuxièmement, le formalisme du modèle de surface RU permet de plus répartir la recharge simulée que le modèle SAMIR. Par ”répartir”, nous entendons ici la capacité à fractionner un événement de recharge sur plusieurs jours. Cela est lié au fait qu’avec le modèle RU, lorsqu’une certaine gamme d’humidité du sol est atteinte, la recharge simulée est divisée par trois. Cela permet de reproduire l’idée que la recharge est théoriquement moins importante lorsque l’humi- dité du sol de la zone racinaire n’est pas à saturation. Ainsi, RU peut simuler une dynamique de recharge moins réactive que SAMIR, et donc un drainage moins réactif, plus adapté à celui observé à AB$_1$ et AB$_2$. Un autre point est à mentionner, mettant en lumière l’importance de spatialiser les modèles de surface pour simuler le drainage. Les valeurs du paramètre Sinter de RU obtenues après calibration sont faibles (17 mm en moyenne en 2021, 61 mm en 2022, alors que les valeurs fournies dans la littérature sont de 138 mm en moyenne ; Jeantet et al. 2021). Cela s’explique par le fait que les modèles basés sur RU ne sont pas spatialisés contrairement à ceux basés sur SAMIR. Pour les [SOURCE: Page_136]

## 6.3. ÉVALUATION DE LA PRÉCISION DES MODÈLES                                                      125

Figure 6.2 – Drainage quotidien et cumulé observé (lignes bleues) et simulé (lignes rouges) par les quatre modèles calibrés avec les données de drainage de la période 2021 (gauche) et 2022 (droite), pour le sous-bassin AB$_2$. Les graphiques du haut montrent la précipitation et l’irrigation. [SOURCE: Page_137]

modèles RU, l’irrigation donnée en forçage à la parcelle moyenne simulée par RU est une irrigation moyenne. Or, en été, l’essentiel de l’irrigation, et donc de la recharge, se produit sur les parcelles de maı̈s étant intensément irriguées (>50 mm/semaine). Les autres parcelles, moins irriguées, ne génèrent pas ou peu de recharge. Le fait que RU utilise une irrigation moyenne, obtenue avec des parcelles peu ou pas irriguées et d’autres intensément irriguées, a pour conséquence que les modèles RU-Reservoir et RU-SIDRA génèrent moins de recharge et donc simulent moins de drainage que les modèles SAMIR-Reservoir et SAMIR-SIDRA. Pour compenser cela, et générer suffisamment de recharge, l’algorithme d’optimisation NSGA-II ajuste Sinter à des valeurs très faibles. [SOURCE: Page_137]

6.4    Évaluation de l’exactitude des modèles Par exactitude, nous entendons ici la capacité des modèles à reproduire le drainage observé en utilisant une calibration par défaut, c’est-à-dire en utilisant des valeurs fournies par la littérature pour leurs paramètres principaux. Pour chacun des paramètres principaux des modèles, la littérature fournit une distribution (avec une valeur moyenne et un écart type). À partir de ces distributions, 2000 échantillons (jeux de paramètres) avec des valeurs aléatoires suivant une distribution normale (lognormale pour les paramètres K et µ de SIDRA) sont préparés avec la méthode de Monte Carlo. Puis, 2000 simulations sont réalisées avec ces 2000 jeux de paramètres. Ainsi, en plus de la capacité des [SOURCE: Page_138]
