Les lignes rouges correspondent au drainage simulé avec des valeurs moyennes pour les paramètres principaux, tandis que les lignes grises correspondent au drainage simulé avec les 2000 jeux de paramètres. Les résultats pour le sous-bassin AB$_2$ sont à retrouver dans l’article de la Section 6.5. Les résultats de l’évaluation de l’exactitude montrent que le modèle SAMIR-Reservoir est le seul capable de reproduire le drainage observé de manière grossière, mais tout de même relative- ment cohérente avec l’observation, et avec un ensemble de simulation moins dispersé que celui des trois autres modèles. Le drainage simulé avec SAMIR-SIDRA montre une certaine cohérence avec le drainage observé, mais présente une réactivité trop importante. Les modèles Ru-Reservoir et RU-SIDRA présentent quant à eux des difficultés à reproduire des quantités suffisantes de drai- nage. Drainage assessment of irrigation districts: on the precision and accuracy of four parsimonious models Pierre Laluet^1, Luis Olivera-Guerra^1,*, Víctor Altés^2,3, Vincent Rivalland^1, Alexis Jeantet^4, Julien Tournebize^4, Omar Cenobio-Cruz^5, Anaïs Barella-Ortiz^5, Pere Quintana-Seguí5, Josep 5   Maria Villar^3, Olivier Merlin^1 [SOURCE: Page_140]

1 Centre d’Etudes Spatiales de la Biosphère (CESBIO), Université de Toulouse, CNES, CNRS, IRD, UPS, Toulouse, France 2 isardSAT, Marie Curie 8-14, Parc Tecnològic Barcelona Activa, Barcelona, Spain 3 Department of Environment and Soil Sciences, Universitat de Lleida, Lleida, Spain 10   4 University of Paris-Saclay, INRAE Jouy-en-Josas – Antony, UR HYCAR, Antony, France 5 Observatori de l’Ebre, Universitat Ramon Llull – CSIC, Roquetes, Spain *now at: Laboratoire des Sciences du Climat et de l’Environnement, CEA-CNRS-UVSQ-UPSACLAY, UMR 8212, IPSL, Gif-sur-Yvette, France [SOURCE: Page_140]

Correspondence: [EMAIL_REDACTED] [SOURCE: Page_140]

15   Abstract. In semi-arid irrigated environments, the agricultural drainage is at the heart of three agro-environmental issues: it is an indicator of water productivity, it is the main control to prevent soil salinization and waterlogging problems, and it is related to the health of downstream ecosystems. Crop water balance models combined with subsurface models can be used to estimate the drainage quantities and dynamics at various spatial scales. However, the precision (capacity of a model to fit the observed drainage using site-specific calibration) and accuracy 20   (capacity of a model to approximate observed drainage using default input parameters) of such models have not yet been assessed in irrigated areas. To fill the gap, this study evaluates four parsimonious drainage models based on the combination of two surface models (RU and SAMIR) and two subsurface models (Reservoir and SIDRA) with varying complexity levels: RU-Reservoir, RU-SIDRA, SAMIR-Reservoir, and SAMIR-SIDRA. All models were applied over two sub-basins of the Algerri-Balaguer irrigation district, northeastern Spain, that are equipped 25   with surface and subsurface drains driving the drained water to general outlets where the discharge is continuously monitored. Results show that RU-Reservoir is the most precise (average KGE (Q$_0$.5) of 0.87), followed by SAMIR- Reservoir (average KGE (Q$_0$.5) of 0.79). However, SAMIR-Reservoir is the most accurate model for providing rough drainage estimates using the default input parameters provided in the literature. [SOURCE: Page_140]

6.5. ARTICLE. DRAINAGE ASSESSMENT OF IRRIGATION DISTRICTS : ON THE PRECISION AND ACCURACY OF FOUR PARSIMONIOUS MODELS                 129 [SOURCE: Page_141]

https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2023-543 Preprint. Discussion started: 24 April 2023 c Author(s) 2023. CC BY 4.0 License. [SOURCE: Page_141]

30   1 Introduction [SOURCE: Page_141]

In the context of ongoing global changes, semi-arid irrigated areas especially face multiple challenges. First, the agricultural water productivity is a critical issue in regions where water resources are under increasing pressure (FAO, 2021). Second, one-third of the world's irrigated land is affected by the soil salinization issue, which is likely to bring a significant loss of arable lands (Singh et al., 2019). Third, the non-point pollution is another issue 35   over irrigated areas, with return flows that may contain high concentrations of nutrients (García-Garizábal et al., 2012) and/or pesticides (Abdi et al., 2021). [SOURCE: Page_141]

At the heart of the above three challenges (water productivity, soil salinization and non-point pollution) lies the agricultural drainage. More than 20% of the total irrigated lands in the world is equipped with drainage systems including open ditches or buried drains (Schultz et al., 2007). Drainage systems are generally installed with the 40   aim to prevent waterlogging during heavy rainfall events (by the sudden rise of groundwater levels) and to facilitate salt leaching. Moreover, the drained water quantity and quality are strong indicators of the agricultural water productivity, and of the possible impact of nitrates, salts, and pesticides concentration on downstream ecosystems (Blann et al., 2009). [SOURCE: Page_141]

In this context, being able to estimate the drained water in irrigated areas is of major importance, whether by 45   monitoring the quantity and quality of the drained water discharged (e.g., Negm et al., 2017), or by developing drainage scenarios that integrate changes in agricultural practices (e.g., Tournebize et al., 2004) or in climatic conditions (e.g., Golmohammadi et al., 2020; Jeantet et al., 2022). To date, only a few studies have dealt with the quantitative estimation of drainage in semi-arid irrigated areas. At the field scale, Ale et al. (2013) compared the ability of the physically-based DRAINMOD (Skaggs et al., 2012) and ADAPT (Gowda et al., 2012) models to 50   simulate monthly drainage in a drip-irrigated plot in the US. The determination coefficient between simulated and observed drainage was 0.90 and 0.85 for ADAPT and DRAINMOD, respectively, for data during a seven-year period. More recently, Feng et al. (2021) simulated the daily drainage with the physically-based Hydrus-2D model in a furrow-irrigated plot and obtained a Nash-Sutcliffe model efficiency coefficient (NSE) value of 0.91 and 0.94 for the calibration and validation year respectively. At a larger spatial scale, Cavero et al. (2012) simulated the 55   monthly drainage of three Mediterranean irrigated catchments (mostly surface irrigation) located in Spain, Algeria, and Turkey, and ranging from 4000 to 10000 hectares. They used the crop water balance model APEX (Gassman et al., 2009) coupled with DRAINMOD over two hydrological years and obtained Root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) ranging from 3.4 mm per month to 25.3 mm per month. At much larger scale, Wen et al. (2020) simulated the monthly drainage over 19 sub-basins in a 1.2 million hectare irrigation district in northern China using an 60   empirical approach based on water table observations. The results showed a mixed performance with an average NSE of 0.64 and a standard deviation of 0.21 for the 2-year calibration period, and an average NSE of 0.34 and a standard deviation of 0.44 for the 2-year validation period. In the same irrigation district, Chang et al. (2021) simulated the annual drainage discharge under different management scenarios using the semi-empirical SAHYSMOD model (Oosterbaan et al., 2005). [SOURCE: Page_141]

65   Although the literature on the agricultural drainage is still limited for semi-arid irrigated areas, there are many scientific papers on the drainage estimation in humid areas, where waterlogging problems are common. The vast [SOURCE: Page_141]

## 130                   CHAPITRE 6. SIMULER LE DRAINAGE DES PÉRIMÈTRES IRRIGUÉS

https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2023-543 Preprint. Discussion started: 24 April 2023 c Author(s) 2023. CC BY 4.0 License. [SOURCE: Page_142]

majority of them use physically-based models such as DRAINMOD (Moursi et al., 2022; Muma et al, 2015), RZWQM$_2$ (Ma et al., 2012; Xian et al., 2017; Jiang et al. 2020), MACRO (Larsbo et al., 2005; Jarvis and Larsbo, 2012), SWAP (van Dam et al., 2008), HydroGeoSphere (De Schepper et al., 2015), and FLUSH (Turunen et al., 70   2013; Nousiainen et al., 2015). Generally, these models are implemented at the plot scale and represent the intermediate processes (e.g., macropore infiltration, deep seepage, water redistribution in the soil profile, rooting distribution, lateral flows) involved in drainage at the daily or hourly time step. They rely on a lot of information for model parameterization, implying a detailed knowledge of the studied site, and potentially numerous parameters to calibrate. For example, Ma et al. (2012) recommend for the RZWQM$_2$ model an independent 75   measurement for 11 parameters, and a calibration for 11 others, out of a total of 24 parameters (the two remaining ones being taken from the literature). In fields where intensive measurement campaigns have been conducted, these models can simulate well the observed drainage at hourly, daily, weekly, or monthly scales. However, due to the need for site-specific calibration (using drainage measurements) to set their relatively numerous input parameters, the application of such models to poorly monitored basins remains limited. [SOURCE: Page_142]

80   With the aim to generalize a drainage model for various agricultural conditions, Henine et al. (2022) proposed a simple semi-empirical drainage model, RU-SIDRA. It combines a surface model (RU) to simulate the daily recharge and a subsurface model (SIDRA) (Lesaffre and Zimmer, 1987; Bouarfa and Zimmer, 2000) to convert the simulated recharge into daily drainage discharge. RU is a water balance model based on a simplified version of the FAO-56 method and relies on a single sensitive parameter only. SIDRA is based on the resolution of a semi- 85   analytical formula derived from the Boussinesq physical equation (Boussinesq, 1904), leading to two main sensitive parameters. The robustness of RU-SIDRA was evaluated by Jeantet et al. (2021) on 22 non-irrigated French fields and sub-basins over 200 hydrological years. It was found that RU-SIDRA performs as well as physically-based models in reproducing daily drainage and is as robust as the latter from one hydrological year to another. However, Jeantet et al. (2021) emphasized a limitation of RU-SIDRA associated with the empirical nature 90   of the RU model. Indeed, in RU, the start of drainage is not systematically well reproduced from year to year. This is potentially due to its poor representation of the processes governing the variation of the soil water stock (e.g., root growth or evapotranspiration). Over irrigated areas, this difficulty is expected to be further exacerbated by the impact of summer crops. In addition, as the physically based-models described previously, RU-SIDRA also relies on a site-specific calibration step using rarely available observed drainage data. [SOURCE: Page_142]

95   Finding the right balance between the simplicity required for a drainage model to be easily applicable over large areas and the complexity required to ensure a sufficient realism of intermediate processes and hence the robustness of drainage estimates in time remains a challenge. In this context, this study seeks to address the following questions: [SOURCE: Page_142]

- Can parsimonious models with different degrees of complexity precisely reproduce the daily drainage in a semi- 100   arid irrigated context with site-specific calibration? [SOURCE: Page_142]

- Can such models with default calibration (with parameter values provided in the literature) reproduce drainage quantities and dynamics, even roughly? [SOURCE: Page_142]

6.5. ARTICLE. DRAINAGE ASSESSMENT OF IRRIGATION DISTRICTS : ON THE PRECISION AND ACCURACY OF FOUR PARSIMONIOUS MODELS                 131 [SOURCE: Page_143]

https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2023-543 Preprint. Discussion started: 24 April 2023 c Author(s) 2023. CC BY 4.0 License. [SOURCE: Page_143]

In this context, we evaluated the precision and accuracy of several parsimonious models based on the RU-SIDRA formalism. By precision and accuracy, it is meant the capacity of each model to predict the drainage after site- 105   specific calibration (using drainage measurements) and by setting the model input parameters to default values found in the literature (without using drainage measurements), respectively. [SOURCE: Page_143]

To cover a range of modeling complexity, we investigate the SAMIR model (Simonneaux et al., 2009) as an alternative to the RU model. SAMIR is more complex than RU as it simulates more processes (e.g., root growth, vegetation development, evaporation, vegetation cover, specific crop water needs and resistance to stress), while 110   remaining parsimonious with only two parameters integrating most of the sensitivity for the recharge simulation (Laluet et al., 2023). We also investigate the Reservoir model as an alternative to the SIDRA model. Reservoir is a fully empirical model driven by a single parameter. It is a simplified version of a module recently incorporated in the SASER (Safran-Surfex-Eaudysee-Rapid) hydrological model (Quintana-Seguí et al., 2017; Vergnes and Habets, 2018; David et al., 2011) by Cenobio-Cruz et al. (2023) who showed its ability to satisfactorily reproduce 115   the low flows (groundwater discharge) observed at 53 hydrological stations in France and Spain. [SOURCE: Page_143]

The combination of both recharge (RU and SAMIR) models and both subsurface (Reservoir and SIDRA) models generates four drainage models by order of increasing complexity: RU-Reservoir (two main parameters), RU- SIDRA (three main parameters), SAMIR-Reservoir (three main parameters), SAMIR-SIDRA (four main parameters). In this study, the precision and accuracy evaluation of the four drainage models are carried out in two 120   sub-basins of the Algerri-Balaguer irrigation district located in the Ebro basin, northeast of Spain. These two sub- basins are both instrumented with flow meters continuously measuring the daily drainage discharge into the main drains. [SOURCE: Page_143]

2.1 Study area and data [SOURCE: Page_145]

135   2.1.1 Study area [SOURCE: Page_145]

The Algerri-Balaguer (AB) irrigation district is located in northeast Spain, 20 km north of the city of Lleida. It is characterized by a semi-arid continental Mediterranean climate with an average annual reference evapotranspiration (ET$_0$) of 1027 mm and precipitation of 380 mm (2000-2021). AB has an area of 8100 hectares of cropland with mainly corn, barley, wheat, fruit trees, and alfalfa. 6800 hectares are equipped for irrigation with 140   sprinklers for annual crops and drip systems for fruit trees. An overview of the AB area is shown in Fig. 2. For an extensive description of the irrigation district in terms of soil, geology, crops, irrigation and drainage system the reader is referred to refer to Altés et al. (2022). [SOURCE: Page_145]

A network of surface (open ditches) and subsurface (buried pipes) drains was installed in the AB district from 1998 to 2017, intercepting a water table relying on a shallow impermeable layer (Altés et al., 2022). Field drains 145   (underground perforated plastic pipes) are connected to main drains that convey the water to general outlets (green dots in Fig. 2). The main drains were installed in the first few years during irrigation implementation and since then field drains are installed progressively on the initiative of each farmer according to their needs. We have no precise information on the surface that has been equipped with field drains or on their spacing. From field obser- vations, we know that the surface drains were dug at a depth of approximately 2 m, as were the main drains. [SOURCE: Page_145]

150   Two of these main drains have been equipped with CTD-10 sensors (Meter Group Inc., Pullman, WA, USA) that continuously measure the water level. They collect drainage water from areas of 116 and 2050 hectares each, forming two sub-basins AB$_1$ and AB$_2$ (see Fig. 2). These areas correspond to the topographic basins formed by the main drains at the CTD-10 sensors locations and were computed using the QGIS software with a 2 m resolution DEM provided by the Cartographic and Geological Institute of Catalonia. Table 1 shows for AB, AB$_1$, and AB$_2$, 155   the area and percentages of the main crop types. Figure 2.b shows the land cover of AB$_1$ and AB$_2$ for 2021. [SOURCE: Page_145]

165   2.1.2 Data [SOURCE: Page_147]

The water levels measured in the AB$_1$ and AB$_2$ outlets are obtained at hourly intervals and converted into daily discharge using the Manning-Strickler equation and the knowledge of the main drain hydraulic characteristics (Altés et al., 2022). The available drainage data used herein cover the period from February 2021 to October 2022 (21 months) for AB$_1$ and from May 2021 to October 2022 (18 months) for AB$_2$. The drainage data of both AB$_1$ 170   and AB$_2$ for the period from May 2021 to October 2022 are presented in Fig. 3, where differences in terms of drainage quantity and dynamics can be observed. [SOURCE: Page_147]

Figure 3. Daily drainage data of AB$_1$ and AB$_2$ for the period from May 2021 to October 2022. [SOURCE: Page_147]

The irrigation data consist of the daily flow of water pumped from a river located next to the AB district (see Fig. 175   2), which is the only supply for the irrigation network. They are provided by the Automatic Hydrological Information System of the Ebro Basin (SAIH). Pumping flow data are aggregated to the weekly scale to consider the potential delay of several days between pumping and application in the field. 5.8% of the volume is removed to account for evaporation loss and leakage, based on a comparison between the water pumped from the river and irrigation data from water meters (Olivera-Guerra et al., 2023). [SOURCE: Page_147]

180   Soil texture is obtained from the 250-meter resolution SoilGrids product (Hengl et al. 2017; Poggio et al. 2021). It is relatively uniform over the AB area and corresponds to a silty clay loam soil (Jahn et al., 2006). [SOURCE: Page_147]

Meteorological data are obtained from five stations belonging to the Catalan Meteorological Station Network. Two of them are located within the AB district, and the three others are located around the area at a maximum distance of 5 km. The mean standard deviation of the instantaneous measurements of precipitation and ET$_0$ made by the 185   five stations is very low. Therefore, the spatial average of precipitation and ET$_0$ measurements is used as forcing at the scale of AB sub-basins. [SOURCE: Page_148]

2.2 Description of the four models [SOURCE: Page_148]

The four models evaluated herein result from the combination of two water balance models (RU and SAMIR) and two drainage discharge models (Reservoir and SIDRA). Their main characteristics are listed in Table 2. [SOURCE: Page_148]

## 2.2.1 SAMIR

The SAMIR model (Simonneaux et al., 2009) is a FAO56 double crop coefficient-based model (FAO-2Kc) (Allen et al., 1998) designed to simulate the crop water balance components for daily ET estimation and crop water 195   requirements by considering the plant and soil water status. It uses i) meteorological forcing variables to calculate ET$_0$ (calculated using the Penman-Monteith equation), ii) precipitation, iii) crop and soil parameters to calculate soil reservoir properties, as well as plant and soil resistance to water stress, and iv) Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) to drive plant development, obtained from the Sentinel-2 satellites with a resolution of 10 m and a revisit of five days. [SOURCE: Page_148]

200   The daily water balance equation simulated with SAMIR is: [SOURCE: Page_148]

𝐷𝑟𝑡 = 𝐷𝑟𝑡−1 + 𝐸𝑇𝑡 − 𝑃𝑡 − 𝐼𝑡 + 𝑅𝑡                                                                               (1) [SOURCE: Page_148]

6.5. ARTICLE. DRAINAGE ASSESSMENT OF IRRIGATION DISTRICTS : ON THE PRECISION AND ACCURACY OF FOUR PARSIMONIOUS MODELS                 137 [SOURCE: Page_149]

https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2023-543 Preprint. Discussion started: 24 April 2023 c Author(s) 2023. CC BY 4.0 License. [SOURCE: Page_149]

where Dr is the root zone depletion, ET the actual evapotranspiration, P the precipitation, I the irrigation, and R the underground recharge. Every term is expressed in mm for the day t (and t-1 for Dr). ET is estimated by multiplying two crop coefficients to ET$_0$ as follows: [SOURCE: Page_149]

205   𝐸𝑇𝑡 = (𝐾𝑐𝑏𝑡 ∙ 𝐾𝑠𝑡 + 𝐾𝑒𝑡 ∙ 𝐾𝑟𝑡 ) ∙ 𝐸𝑇0 𝑡                                                                     (2) [SOURCE: Page_149]

where ET$_0$·Kcb·Ks is the water transpired by plants (T, mm), and ET$_0$·Ke·Kr the soil evaporation (E, mm). Kcb (-) is the basal crop coefficient governing the potential crop transpiration. It is estimated from a linear relationship with NDVI. Ks (-) is the water stress coefficient reducing the potential transpiration, Ke (-) the potential soil evaporation coefficient, and Kr (-) the evaporation reduction coefficient. [SOURCE: Page_149]

210   Kr is calculated with a pedotransfer function using clay and sand fractions that was derived and evaluated over a variety of sites (Lehmann et al., 2018; Merlin et al., 2016) and recently implemented into SAMIR by Amazirh et al. (2021). [SOURCE: Page_149]

Ks is calculated based on the daily computation of the water balance in the root-zone layer, as follows: [SOURCE: Page_149]

𝑇𝐴𝑊 −𝐷𝑟 𝐾𝑠𝑡 = 𝑇𝐴𝑊 𝑡(1−𝑝)𝑡                                                                                           (3) 𝑡 [SOURCE: Page_149]

215   where Dr is calculated from the daily water balance according to Eq. (1), TAW (mm) is the maximum available water in the root zone and p (-) is the fraction of TAW that a crop can extract without facing water stress. Allen et al. (1998) suggests that p controls the water depth threshold below which irrigation should be triggered to avoid crop water stress, by keeping Dr smaller than TAW·p (and thus Ks equal to 1). TAW is estimated as follows: [SOURCE: Page_149]

𝑇𝐴𝑊𝑡 = (𝑆𝑀𝐹𝐶 − 𝑆𝑀𝑊𝑃 ) ∙ 𝑍𝑟𝑡                                                                                 (4) [SOURCE: Page_149]

220   where SMFC (m^3 m-3) is the soil moisture at field capacity and SMWP (m^3 m-3) the soil moisture at the wilting point, both derived from the soil texture by applying the pedotransfer function proposed by Román-Dobarco et al. (2019). Zr (mm) is the rooting depth that varies between a minimum value (set to 100 mm for annual crops) and a crop- dependent maximum value (reached at the maximum NDVI of the simulated field). [SOURCE: Page_149]

A spatialized version of SAMIR at the plot-scale was recently developed and is used in this study to simulate 225   recharge at AB$_1$ and AB$_2$. More details on the methodology behind this spatialization can be found in Olivera- Guerra et al. (2023). [SOURCE: Page_149]

To simulate plot-scale irrigation using SAMIR, we used the method proposed by Olivera-Guerra et al. (2023), which consists of inverting two time-varying SAMIR irrigation parameters from the irrigation data measured at the pumping station. By applying the inverted parameters to each irrigated field, and by aggregating the resulting 230   simulations over the entire AB district, the simulated irrigation volumes and timing were found quite close to those measured at the pumping station (RMSD < 0.70 mm d-1 on average for six irrigation seasons). The values of the SAMIR irrigation parameters found by Olivera-Guerra et al. (2023) for the AB district were used herein for 2021 and 2022. The plot-scale irrigations simulated by SAMIR are then averaged for AB$_1$ and AB$_2$ to be used as forcing in the RU model (as RU is not spatialized). [SOURCE: Page_149]

## 235   2.2.2 RU

RU is a water balance model designed to simulate the recharge of the water table. It is one of the components of the RU-SIDRA model introduced by Henine et al. (2022). In contrast to SAMIR, RU has not been designed to precisely reproduce ET by simulating plant phenology or processes related to evaporation. Its purpose is rather to reproduce the correct amount of recharge to be converted into drainage with the SIDRA model. While a detailed 240   description of the model can be found in Henine et al. (2022) and its evaluation in Jeantet et al. (2021), only a general overview is provided here. [SOURCE: Page_150]

RU uses as input precipitation, irrigation, ET$_0$, and soil texture type (for default parameter values). It is composed of a module simulating the net infiltration (Pnet, mm) and a soil reservoir module transforming Pnet into recharge R. [SOURCE: Page_150]

245   Pnet is calculated as follows: [SOURCE: Page_150]

𝑃𝑛𝑒𝑡 𝑡 = 𝑃𝑡 + 𝐼𝑡 − 𝐶𝐸𝑇𝑡                                                                                          (5) [SOURCE: Page_150]

With CET (mm) being the corrected ET, which is computed as follows: [SOURCE: Page_150]

−𝑆𝑅𝐹𝑈 −𝑆𝑡 [SOURCE: Page_150]

𝐶𝐸𝑇𝑡 = { 𝐸𝑇0𝑡 ∙ 𝑒                𝑖𝑓 𝑆𝑡 < 𝑆𝑅𝐹𝑈 𝑆𝑡 (6) 𝐸𝑇0𝑡                     𝑖𝑓 𝑆𝑡 ≥ 𝑆𝑅𝐹𝑈 [SOURCE: Page_150]

where St (mm) is the current water level in the soil reservoir on day t and SRFU (mm) a water level threshold 250   triggering the plant water stress limiting ET$_0$. SRFU is 0.4·Sinter with Sinter (mm) being a threshold in the soil reservoir that triggers recharge, analogous to SMFC in SAMIR. [SOURCE: Page_150]

The soil reservoir module is designed to simulate recharge (R) depending on three stages related to the amount of water in the soil reservoir (S): [SOURCE: Page_150]

𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒 1: 𝑆𝑡 < 𝑆𝑖𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑟 ; 𝑅𝑡 = 0                                                                                    (7) [SOURCE: Page_150]

255   𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒 2: 𝑆𝑡 ∈ [𝑆𝑖𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑟 ; 𝑆𝑚𝑎𝑥 ] ; 𝑅𝑡 = 𝛽 ∙ 𝑃𝑛𝑒𝑡𝑡                                                                  (8) [SOURCE: Page_150]

With Smax (mm) being the water level below which recharge occurs with a reduction coefficient β (−) and calculated as follows: [SOURCE: Page_150]

𝑆𝑚𝑎𝑥 = 𝑆𝑖𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑟 + 𝑆𝐼𝐷𝑆                                                                                             (9) [SOURCE: Page_150]

Where SIDS (mm) is the intense drainage season reservoir level (Jeantet et al., 2021). Henine et al. (2022) and Chelil 260   et al. (2022) found that both SIDS and β are not significantly sensitive. Based on the values used in Jeantet et al. (2021), SIDS was set to 20 mm and β to 0.33. [SOURCE: Page_150]

𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒 3: 𝑆𝑡 > 𝑆𝑚𝑎𝑥 ; 𝑅𝑡 = 𝑃𝑛𝑒𝑡𝑡                                                                                  (10) [SOURCE: Page_150]

## 265   2.2.3 SIDRA

SIDRA is a physically-based model designed to calculate the drainage flow of a drained plot or a drained sub- basin. It is based on the resolution of a semi-analytical formula derived from the Boussinesq equation, which leads to Eq. (11) and Eq. (12). For a complete description of SIDRA, readers are referred to Tournebize et al. (2004), Henine et al. (2022), and Zimmer et al. (2023). [SOURCE: Page_151]

270   First, the water table level variation under the influence of recharge (R) and drainage is computed as follows: [SOURCE: Page_151]

ℎ𝑡 2 𝑑ℎ𝑡  𝑅𝑡 −𝐾 2                       𝑑ℎ = 𝐶µ 𝐿         ; ℎ𝑡+1 = ℎ𝑡 + 𝑑 𝑡                                                                       (11) 𝑑𝑡                                  𝑡 [SOURCE: Page_151]

where h is the water table (m), K the horizontal hydraulic conductivity (m d-1), μ the drainable porosity (m^3 m-3), and C a water table shape factor (-) equal to 0.904. h is bounded between 0 and 1.5 (the average drain depth assumed at AB). The drainage of the water table into buried pipes or open drains, leading to drainage flow Q, is 275   calculated as follows: [SOURCE: Page_151]

ℎ² 𝑄𝑡 = 𝐴𝐾       + (1 − 𝐴)𝑅𝑡                                                                                   (12) 𝐿² [SOURCE: Page_151]

where L is the half of the drain spacing (or mid-drain spacing, m) and A a water table shape factor (-) equal to 0.896. As we do not have precise information on the field drains location and the proportion of the surface actually equipped with them at AB, L can be either calibrated with drainage data, or set to a value frequently found in the 280   literature (generally comprise between 3 and 12 m). [SOURCE: Page_151]

Boussinesq's equation assumes that buried pipes and open drains rest on an impermeable layer, meaning that the entire water table could be drained after a given period without rain or irrigation. The hydrogeological configuration of the AB district, with the presence of a shallow impervious layer, allows us to assume that this condition is respected. [SOURCE: Page_151]

285   SIDRA is not spatialized; therefore, when combined with SAMIR (which is spatialized, unlike RU), it uses as input the average daily recharge from all the simulated plots of AB$_1$ and AB$_2$. [SOURCE: Page_151]

2.2.4 Reservoir [SOURCE: Page_151]

Reservoir (Cenobio-Cruz et al., 2023) is a conceptual model designed to reproduce the delay between the recharge and the water table draining into a river, buried pipes, or open drains. The idea of this model is that a reservoir 290   filled by recharge is drained according to a linear relationship between the water level Z (mm) and a depletion coefficient k (-). It can be expressed as follows: [SOURCE: Page_151]

𝑄𝑡 = 𝑍𝑡 ∙ 𝑘                                                                                                (13) [SOURCE: Page_151]

https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2023-543 Preprint. Discussion started: 24 April 2023 c Author(s) 2023. CC BY 4.0 License. [SOURCE: Page_152]

Cenobio-Cruz et al. (2023) incorporated a reservoir size parameter to simulate overflow and generate quick flows. We decided not to include this parameter to make the Reservoir model as simple as possible. [SOURCE: Page_152]

295   2.2.5 Initialization of the state variables [SOURCE: Page_152]

The four models RU-Reservoir, RU-SIDRA, SAMIR-Reservoir, and SAMIR-SIDRA require initialization of their state variables. These variables were initialized with a 12-month spin-up simulation using data from 2020. SAMIR initializes the depletion parameters of the soil and surface reservoirs, RU the water level in the soil reservoir, SIDRA the water table level, and Reservoir the water level in the conceptual reservoir. [SOURCE: Page_152]

300   2.2.6 Sensitivity of model parameters [SOURCE: Page_152]

Laluet et al. (2023) conducted an extensive sensitivity analysis of ET and recharge simulated by SAMIR over a wide range of agro-pedoclimatic conditions. Two of the nine parameters were found to dominate the model sensitivity: aKcb governing the relationship between NDVI and Kcb (related to T demand), and Zrmax being the maximum rooting depth governing the size of the root zone reservoir. [SOURCE: Page_152]

305   Henine et al. (2022) and Chelil et al. (2022) analyzed the sensitivity of the RU-SIDRA parameters for drainage simulation on two different plots. They both showed that for the RU model, the Sinter parameter controls most of the model sensitivity, and that for SIDRA it is K and μ. [SOURCE: Page_152]

2.3 Strategy for evaluating the models’ precision [SOURCE: Page_152]

It is reminded that by precision it is meant the ability of a model to approximate the observed drainage data as 310   closely as possible by means of site-specific calibration (using drainage measurements). The most sensitive parameters of the four models were calibrated using an automatic calibration algorithm. Since we do not have information on the mid-drain spacing on AB, we calibrated the L parameter, bringing the number of parameters to be calibrated for RU-SIDRA to four, and for SAMIR-Reservoir to five. Indeed, although Chelil et al. (2022) showed that L is not very sensitive when it varies between 3.5 m and 6 m, its uncertainty within the AB district is 315   large enough for it to be significantly sensitive. The other less sensitive parameters are fixed at the default values given in the literature. In an effort to analyze the variability of the parameters from one hydrological year to the next, we split the data into a 12-month period named “2021 period”, and a period with the remaining months (9 months for AB$_1$, 6 months for AB$_2$) named “2022 period”. [SOURCE: Page_152]

The calibration method used is the multi-objective Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm (NSGA-II) (Deb et 320   al., 2002). For the case of SAMIR, which simulates both irrigation and recharge, we use a multi-objective method to ensure that the calibration of aKcb and Zrmax parameters does not significantly modify the simulated irrigation. Therefore, for both SAMIR-Reservoir and SAMIR-SIDRA, drainage and irrigation are optimized together, whereas for both RU-Reservoir and RU-SIDRA, only drainage is optimized (an averaged irrigation is given as forcing in this case as RU cannot simulate irrigation). NSGA-II is one of the most widely used multi-objective 325   algorithms. It implements a fast non-dominant sorting approach to discriminate solutions based on the concept of dominance and Pareto optimality. It provides a set of optimal non-dominated solutions (set of parameters), allowing the user to choose the best solution according to his priorities. In the SAMIR case, the best solution would [SOURCE: Page_152]

6.5. ARTICLE. DRAINAGE ASSESSMENT OF IRRIGATION DISTRICTS : ON THE PRECISION AND ACCURACY OF FOUR PARSIMONIOUS MODELS                 141 [SOURCE: Page_153]

https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2023-543 Preprint. Discussion started: 24 April 2023 c Author(s) 2023. CC BY 4.0 License. [SOURCE: Page_153]

be the one that simulates the most precise drainage, provided that it simulates irrigation consistent with the observed data at the pumping station. Readers are referred to Deb et al. (2002), Bekele and Nicklow (2007), and 330   Shafii and De Smedt (2008) for a detailed description of the algorithm. [SOURCE: Page_153]

NSGA-II requires a distribution provided by the user for each calibrated parameter. The distribution and references used for each model are provided in Table 3. For the K and µ parameters of SIDRA, the same distribution as in Jeantet et al. (2021) is used because they are derived from field measurements performed on 15 silty soils, being similar to the soil texture of AB$_1$ and AB$_2$. For the k parameter of Reservoir, we use a normal distribution with a 335   mean of 0.02, as this is the average value obtained by Cenobio-Cruz et al. (2023) on approximately 25 watersheds in northern Spain. [SOURCE: Page_153]

For drainage calibration, the objective function Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) (Gupta et al., 2009) is used: [SOURCE: Page_153]

𝐾𝐺𝐸 = 1 − √(𝑟 − 1)2 + (𝛼 − 1)2 + (𝛿 − 1)²                                                                   (14) [SOURCE: Page_153]

where r is the Pearson’s correlation coefficient, α the bias component, and δ the ratio of the discharge variance: [SOURCE: Page_153]

𝑚𝑠                      𝜎𝑠 340   𝛼=        𝑎𝑛𝑑 𝛿 =                                                                                           (15) 𝑚𝑜                      𝜎𝑜 [SOURCE: Page_153]

where m and σ are the mean and standard deviation, respectively. Subscripts s and o represent the simulated and observed flow, respectively. [SOURCE: Page_153]

Since KGE tends to place more weight on high flows (Santos et al., 2018), we chose to use KGE (Q$_0$.5). KGE (Q$_0$.5) is the KGE calculated from the squared roots of simulated and observed drainage, allowing the weights between 345   high and low flows to be more balanced. Following Jeantet et al. (2021), we consider simulations as “excellent” when KGE (Q$_0$.5) is larger than 0.8, "very good" when it is larger than 0.7, "good" when it is larger than 0.6, "acceptable" when it is between 0.5 and 0.6, and “unsatisfactory” when it is below 0.5. Furthermore, to get a reference in mind, a KGE of -0.41 is equivalent to having a simulation performance equal to the average of the observed data (Knoben et al., 2019). [SOURCE: Page_153]

350   The RMSD objective function is used for irrigation calibration: [SOURCE: Page_153]

𝑗 ∑       (ŷ𝑖 −𝑦𝑖 )² 𝑅𝑀𝑆𝐷 = √ 𝑖=1 𝑗                                                                                              (16) [SOURCE: Page_153]

where j is the number of days in the simulated time series, i is one day of the time series, ŷi is the simulated time series, and yi is the reference time series. We consider irrigation to be well simulated when the RMSD calculated between the irrigation measured at the pumping station and the one simulated by SAMIR for all the plots in AB is 355   below 0.70 mm d-1. This value corresponds to the RMSD found on average from 2017 to 2021 by Olivera-Guerra et al. (2023). [SOURCE: Page_153]

2.4 Strategy for evaluating the models’ accuracy [SOURCE: Page_154]

Complementarily to the evaluation of the models’ precision, this study also aims to assess the accuracy of the four models. It is reminded that by accuracy we mean the ability of a model to approximate the observed data as closely as possible, by relying only on default values given by the literature for its main parameters, i.e., without any site- 365   specific calibration step. [SOURCE: Page_154]

To this end, for each of the four models, 2000 sets of their most sensitive parameters are generated randomly by means of a Monte Carlo sampling, using the distributions presented in Table 3. Unlike the previous step, here the value of the mid-drain spacing L is set to 6 m since it is a value frequently found in the literature. In addition, in order to focus only on the drainage accuracy evaluation, the irrigation obtained with SAMIR during the precision 370   evaluation step is injected into SAMIR as a forcing. The KGE (Q 0.5) obtained with a simulation performed with average default parameters is calculated, and the ensemble generated by the 2000 Monte-Carlo simulations is analyzed. [SOURCE: Page_154]

3 Results and discussion 375 3.1 Precision evaluation [SOURCE: Page_154]

In this section we will first give a quick overview of the irrigation simulated by SAMIR and used as a forcing by RU. The precision of the drainage simulated by each model is then presented. Finally, we will explain why the model precision differs between the four models and provide some recommendations and perspectives. [SOURCE: Page_154]

420   3.1.3 Why are Reservoir-based models more precise? [SOURCE: Page_159]

The better performance of the site-calibrated RU-Reservoir and SAMIR-Reservoir models is explained by the differences in the formalism of Reservoir and SIDRA and by the low responsiveness of the AB$_1$ and AB$_2$ hydrosystems. Indeed, SIDRA was designed to simulate flow peaks followed by relatively steep recession curves. In contrast, Reservoir does not simulate peaks, and generates flow according to a depletion coefficient k that can 425   be very low. However, the measured drainage dynamics for AB$_1$ and AB$_2$ are representative of low-responsive hydrosystems. This can be seen in Fig. 4 and 5 where the 40 mm rainfall in December 2021 generates a peak of less than 1 mm d-1 for both sub-basins, followed by a recession curve being quite smooth with a discharge that never reaches 0 during the hydrological year. In comparison, the data used by Jeantet et al. (2021) from 22 French experimental sites, accounting for nearly 200 hydrological years, show winter peaks exceeding 20 mm d-1 in most 430   of the studied years, followed by steep recession curves where 0 flow is reached in a few weeks. Therefore, the Reservoir model is favored by the low responsiveness of the AB$_1$ and AB$_2$ hydrosystems, and this is especially true for AB$_1$. The SIDRA model shows a better precision for AB$_2$ than for AB$_1$ because AB$_2$ is more responsive with larger amounts of discharge. In addition, the values of the Reservoir depletion coefficient k are low at our sites (0.009 on average) compared to those obtained by Cenobio-Cruz et al. (2022) (0.02 on average), which again 435   reflects the relatively low responsiveness of the studied area. [SOURCE: Page_159]

This low responsiveness is not explained by the soil, since the mean calibrated values of K and μ (0.81 m d-1 and 0.11 m^3 m-3, respectively; see Table 6) are consistent with the order of magnitude found in Jeantet et al. (2021) for a similar soil type (K from 0.1 to 1.8 m d-1, and μ from 0.05 to 0.08 m^3 m-3). The explanation seems to lie in the fact that the surfaces of AB$_1$ and AB$_2$ are not fully equipped with field drains. On non-equipped plots, the transfer 440   time would be longer from the recharge location to the main drain. The values of the calibrated mid-drain spacing L support this assumption, with an average of 37 m (see Table 6), being a value that could represent an average between low L values for plots equipped with field drains, and high L values for plots that are not. [SOURCE: Page_159]

3.1.4 Why are RU-based models more precise? [SOURCE: Page_159]

445   To understand the better performance of the site-calibrated RU-Reservoir and RU-SIDRA models, in comparison with SAMIR-Reservoir and SAMIR-SIDRA, respectively, it is again necessary to look at the differences in formalism between RU and SAMIR. Indeed, RU, unlike SAMIR, has a stage during which a reduction factor β of 0.33 is applied to the recharge (Eq. (8), this stage is triggered with the water level in the soil reservoir). In AB$_1$ and AB$_2$, this stage is triggered in particular during the irrigation season and results in the spread of recharge 450   amounts. This benefits RU-SIDRA, which, owing to the lower recharge events simulated by RU, generates lower peaks consistent with the drainage observations. This process is well illustrated in Fig. 4.d, where RU-SIDRA simulates numerous small peaks during the irrigation period, allowing better matching of the observations, whereas in Fig. 4.h, SAMIR-SIDRA simulates larger and fewer peaks. [SOURCE: Page_159]

Furthermore, the Sinter values of RU obtained through calibration are very low (17 mm on average for the 2021 455   period and 61 mm for the 2022 period; see Table 5) compared with those obtained by Jeantet et al. (2021) (138 mm on average). This is due to the fact that the RU-based models are not spatialized and use an average irrigation [SOURCE: Page_159]

## 148                   CHAPITRE 6. SIMULER LE DRAINAGE DES PÉRIMÈTRES IRRIGUÉS

https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2023-543 Preprint. Discussion started: 24 April 2023 c Author(s) 2023. CC BY 4.0 License. [SOURCE: Page_160]

derived from the irrigation simulated by SAMIR whether for intensely irrigated corn plots generating a lot of recharge, or for non-irrigated plots generating no recharge. Because they simulate an average plot using average irrigation, RU-based models simulate less recharge. To compensate for this, the NSGA-II optimization algorithm 460   finds low Sinter values in order to reduce the reservoir size, and therefore the ET, resulting in increasing the recharge. This explains the low Sinter values retrieved over AB$_1$ and AB$_2$. [SOURCE: Page_160]

3.1.5 Recommendations and perspectives [SOURCE: Page_160]

Based on the results obtained over AB by the four models with varying complexity levels, we recommend the use of RU-Reservoir when drainage data are available for calibration. The simplest model can reproduce the drainage 465   observed at both the AB$_1$ and AB$_2$ outlets fairly well. In fact, the RU-Reservoir model efficiently combines the performance of RU (allowing a better temporal distribution of recharge than SAMIR) and Reservoir (offering drainage simulations with relatively low responsive dynamics), which fits perfectly with the present study. However, if a study is concerned with a more responsive hydrosystem with larger peaks and steeper recession curves, we would recommend the use of RU-SIDRA. Indeed, for the AB$_2$ sub-basin, which is slightly more 470   responsive than AB$_1$, RU-SIDRA shows during the 2021 period (Fig. 5.c) a precision comparable to that of RU- Reservoir (Fig. 5.a). This leads us to assume that RU-SIDRA could be more appropriate than RU-Reservoir for even more responsive hydrosystems. [SOURCE: Page_160]

Since RU is not spatialized and has a very simple formalism, the models based on it are simpler to run and require fewer resources than those based on SAMIR. However, they do not take into account the spatial heterogeneity in 475   terms of irrigation generally encountered in irrigated sub-basins, resulting in very low Sinter calibrated values in order to simulate enough recharge. A spatialization of the RU-based models with irrigation data for each plot would lead to higher calibrated Sinter values more consistent with those proposed in Jeantet et al. (2021). However, RU, unlike SAMIR, cannot simulate irrigation and its spatialization would then require plot-scale irrigation data that are rarely available. [SOURCE: Page_160]

480   Note that in some cases, SAMIR shows a relatively low KGE (Q$_0$.5) and difficulties in reproducing the right amount of drainage (see Fig. 4.d, 4.h, and 5.e). Modifying the SAMIR formalism by taking inspiration from RU and adding a stage related to the soil water availability in which recharge is limited by a factor β could help improve the precision of SAMIR-SIDRA and SAMIR-Reservoir. [SOURCE: Page_160]

3.2 Accuracy evaluation [SOURCE: Page_160]

485   Figures 6 and 7 show for each of the 16 model/sub-basin/period combinations the drainage simulated by using the mean values of default parameters as input to each model (red line), and the 2000 model runs from randomly generated input parameters sets within pre-defined distributions provided by the literature (gray lines). Table 7 summarizes the KGE (Q$_0$.5) obtained with the average default parameters. It indicates that all the 16 cases present "unsatisfactory" KGE (Q$_0$.5) values (below 0.5). Moreover, nine cases show KGE (Q$_0$.5) lower than -0.41, the value 490   corresponding to the KGE obtained with the temporal average of the observed data. [SOURCE: Page_160]

RU-Reservoir shows relatively satisfactory KGE (Q$_0$.5) for the 2022 period (0.22 for AB$_1$ and 0.29 for AB$_2$). However, when looking at the drainage dynamics and amounts illustrated in Fig. 6.b and 7.b it appears that these [SOURCE: Page_160]

SAMIR-Reservoir shows a relatively good KGE (Q$_0$.5) for AB$_2$ for the period 2022 (0.29). Furthermore, 495   the timing and quantities that SAMIR-Reservoir simulated for AB$_1$ for both periods 2021 and 2022, as well as for AB$_2$ for the 2021 period, are more consistent than those simulated by the other three models. 3.2.1 Accuracy of RU-Reservoir and RU-SIDRA [SOURCE: Page_163]

Figures 6.a, 6.c, 7.a, and 7.c show that the RU-based models do not simulate any discharge for the 2021 period 510   with the average default parameters (red lines). This is related to the fact that, in a context where RU is not spatialized while irrigation is spatially heterogeneous, the optimal Sinter value to generate sufficient recharge is lower than those given in the literature. The Sinter values taken from the literature for the accuracy evaluation are then too high to simulate enough recharge. For the 2022 period, relatively small amounts of drainage discharge are however simulated during the irrigation period because the irrigation amounts applied in 2022 are significantly 515   larger than in 2021 (about 100 mm more for the period from May to October). [SOURCE: Page_163]

3.2.2 Accuracy of SAMIR-SIDRA [SOURCE: Page_163]

Figures 6 and 7 show that with average default parameter values, the SAMIR-based models simulate the drainage dynamics with some consistency with the irrigation season and the rain events, for both 2021 and 2022 periods. However, SAMIR-SIDRA shows a lower performance than SAMIR-Reservoir. Several factors may explain this 520   result. First, although they are physical parameters, the values of the SIDRA parameters K and μ found in the literature do not necessarily correspond to their optimal values for a given site. Second, SIDRA is more appropriate for more responsive hydrosystems than AB$_1$ and AB$_2$. Finally, the lack of information on the mid-drain spacing L on the AB district led us to set it at 6 m, whereas when calibrated on AB$_1$ and AB$_2$ this parameter is on average 37 m (considering the plots not equipped with field drains). This lower L value results in a high reactivity of the 525   simulated drainage. [SOURCE: Page_163]

3.2.3 Accuracy of SAMIR-Reservoir [SOURCE: Page_163]

Figures 6.e, 6.f, 7.e, and 7.f. show that the drainage simulated by SAMIR-Reservoir with average default parameter values is more consistent with the observed drainage than the other three models. It also presents less variability within the 2000 simulations ensemble. Fig.7.e shows that SAMIR-Reservoir simulates particularly well the 530   drainage dynamics and quantities for the AB$_2$ sub-basin during the 2021 period. For AB$_1$ during the 2021 and 2022 periods, and for AB$_2$ during the 2022 period, when the discharge is lower, SAMIR-Reservoir tends to overestimate the drainage. [SOURCE: Page_163]

## 152                   CHAPITRE 6. SIMULER LE DRAINAGE DES PÉRIMÈTRES IRRIGUÉS

https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2023-543 Preprint. Discussion started: 24 April 2023 c Author(s) 2023. CC BY 4.0 License. [SOURCE: Page_164]

The SAMIR-Reservoir accuracy varies spatially between AB$_1$ and AB$_2$ and temporally between the 2021 and 2022 periods. These differences reflect the semi-empirical nature of SAMIR and Reservoir models. Indeed, they 535   can be attributed to the impact of unrepresented processes (e.g., lateral flows) or misrepresentation of ET and recharge processes in unusual situations (e.g., 2022 drought and heat waves). Especially the lateral flow is fully neglected by SAMIR. Such subsurface flows may come from outside sub-basins boundaries and contribute significantly to the sub-basin discharge measured at the outlet, depending on the hydrometeorological conditions encountered in a given year. Note that representing subsurface lateral flows would require more complex models 540   than those tested in this study and additional data (e.g., piezometric), which are currently unavailable in the study area. [SOURCE: Page_164]

3.2.4 Recommendations and perspectives [SOURCE: Page_164]

Due to the semi-empirical nature of the four models investigated in this study, it is difficult to reproduce the drainage discharge with default parameters from the literature. A limitation of RU-based models is their lack of 545   spatialization, leading to the use of an average irrigation in forcing, while the irrigation of AB$_1$ and AB$_2$ sub- basins is spatially heterogeneous. This results in RU not having enough irrigation to generate a correct amount of recharge with the Sinter values suggested in the literature (being too high). One way to overcome this would be to spatialize RU with irrigation data at each plot, but these data are rarely available. [SOURCE: Page_164]

SAMIR-Reservoir offers a certain consistency with the observed data and could then provide an approximate idea 550   of the drainage dynamics and amount occurring in an ungauged irrigated sub-catchment. A way to improve the robustness of SAMIR-Reservoir could be to investigate a link between the k parameter and the soil texture or the characteristics of the drainage network (drain depth, mid-drain spacing, and drained surface). [SOURCE: Page_164]

4 Conclusion [SOURCE: Page_164]

555   Estimating the drainage in semi-arid irrigation conditions is of great importance to prevent soil salinization issues, and to assess the water productivity and the irrigation impact on downstream ecosystems. A few studies have used physically-based models to simulate drainage in irrigated context. However, these models have many parameters requiring extensive data that are rarely available. In this paper, we thus assessed the capacity of four parsimonious semi-empirical models to simulate drainage at the scale of two sub-basins of the AB district, northeastern Spain. 560   The four models are built from the combination of two surface models (RU and SAMIR) and two subsurface models (Reservoir and SIDRA) with varying complexity levels: RU-Reservoir (two main parameters), RU-SIDRA (three main parameters), SAMIR-Reservoir (three main parameters) and SAMIR-SIDRA (four main parameters). SAMIR is based on the FAO-56 ET and crop water balance formulations relying on two main sensitive parameters, while RU is a simplified version of the FAO-56 relying on a single sensitive parameter only. SIDRA solves the 565   Boussinesq equation from two main sensitive parameters, while Reservoir is an empirical drainage model based on a single depletion parameter only. [SOURCE: Page_164]

The precision of the four models, i.e., their ability to reproduce observed drainage data with a site-specific calibration, was first evaluated. An optimal calibration approach was implemented for each model and each sub- [SOURCE: Page_164]

6.5. ARTICLE. DRAINAGE ASSESSMENT OF IRRIGATION DISTRICTS : ON THE PRECISION AND ACCURACY OF FOUR PARSIMONIOUS MODELS                 153 [SOURCE: Page_165]

https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2023-543 Preprint. Discussion started: 24 April 2023 c Author(s) 2023. CC BY 4.0 License. [SOURCE: Page_165]

basin using the multi-objective genetic algorithm NSGA-II. The comparison between the drainage simulated by 570   site-specific calibrated models and observations indicates that RU-Reservoir presents a better precision, followed closely by SAMIR-Reservoir. This is explained by the fact that Reservoir model is well suited to represent the low responsiveness of both studied sub-basins, and that RU model manages to artificially better spread out the recharge events during the irrigation period than SAMIR model. [SOURCE: Page_165]

The point is that the drainage observations required to undertake a site-specific calibration are rarely available. 575   Therefore, the accuracy of the four models was also evaluated. By accuracy, it is meant the ability of the four models to reproduce the observed drainage using default parameter values provided by the literature. The comparison between the drainage simulated by default-calibrated models and observations indicates that SAMIR- Reservoir is the only model among the four tested capable of providing a rough estimate of the drainage dynamics and amounts from default parameters. [SOURCE: Page_165]

580   However, it was found that the accuracy of SAMIR-Reservoir is quite variable from one sub-basin to another and from one hydrological year to another. Therefore, calibration strategies are still needed to reduce uncertainties in SAMIR-Reservoir drainage estimates in sub-basins with contrasted conditions. In addition, better constraining the value of the Reservoir's depletion coefficient k, especially by seeking a link with soil texture, or with the characteristics of the drainage network, should be investigated in future studies to improve the accuracy of SAMIR- 585   Reservoir. [SOURCE: Page_165]

Furthermore, our study took place in an irrigation district where the water use is known and accurately monitored through the pumping data. Such irrigation data are rarely available in practice, and no model can predict drainage accurately based on inaccurate irrigation forcing, regardless of the model calibration issue. It is hence crucial to develop tools to retrieve the irrigation practices, notably at the integrated spatial scales of sub-basin or irrigation 590   district. To this end, many recent works seek to assimilate satellite products of soil moisture or ET in crop water balance models at a range of scales (e.g., Ouaadi et al., 2021; Massari et al., 2021; Dari et al., 2022; Olivera-Guerra et al., 2020). The coupling of such remote sensing approaches with surface and subsurface models is likely to improve the predictive capabilities of drainage on irrigated areas. [SOURCE: Page_165]

595   Code availability. All Python codes will be provided by the corresponding author upon request. The Python package spotpy (Houska et al., 2015) used for the NSGA-II multi-objective optimization is available at https://github.com/thouska/spotpy. [SOURCE: Page_165]

Data availability. Drainage data are not publicly available. Daily precipitation and ET$_0$ data were provided by the Meteorological Service of Catalonia and are available at https://ruralcat.gencat.cat/agrometeo.estacions (accessed 600   2 March 2023). ## 160                 CHAPITRE 6. SIMULER LE DRAINAGE DES PÉRIMÈTRES IRRIGUÉS

6.6      Conclusion, limites, et perspectives L’évaluation de la précision des quatre modèles de drainage a montré qu’ils affichent tous de bonnes performances lorsqu’ils sont calibrés sur les données de drainage des sous-bassins AB$_1$ et AB$_2$. Le modèle le plus simple, RU-Reservoir, est celui qui présente les meilleures performances (KGE (Q$_0$.5 ) moyen de 0.87). L’évaluation de l’exactitude a montré qu’un seul modèle, SAMIR- Reservoir, est capable de reproduire grossièrement le drainage observé aux sous-bassins AB$_1$ et AB$_2$, lorsque des valeurs issues de la littérature sont utilisées pour renseigner ses trois paramètres principaux. Ce travail a également mis en lumière l’importance de simuler la recharge de manière spatia- lisée (à l’échelle de la parcelle) afin de simuler suffisamment de drainage, et donc la nécessité de simuler l’irrigation à l’échelle de la parcelle également. En effet, au sein d’un périmètre irrigué, l’irrigation est spatialement hétérogène, avec l’essentiel du drainage provenant d’un nombre limité de parcelles étant les plus irriguées. En ne spatialisant pas les modèles de surface, les parcelles fortement irriguées, qui contribuent le plus à la recharge, ne sont pas adéquatement représentées. Cela conduit à une sous-estimation de la recharge, et, par conséquent, du drainage. Des différences en termes de performances des modèles d’un sous-bassin à l’autre apparaissent. Cela illustre la nature semi-empirique des modèles utilisés. En effet, ces différences peuvent être attribuées à des processus non représentés tels que des flux souterrains latéraux pouvant prove- nir de l’extérieur des limites des sous-bassins AB$_1$ et AB$_2$. Ceci est une hypothèse qu’il faudrait vérifier, et qui, pour ce faire, nécessiterait des données piézométriques. [SOURCE: Page_172]

Nous esquissons ici quelques limites et perspectives de ce travail, mais celles-ci sont présentées de manière plus détaillée et approfondie dans la Section 7. - Il serait intéressant d’évaluer les modèles sur d’autres sous-bassins instrumentés, afin d’éva- luer dans quelles mesures les conclusions de ce travail s’appliquent à d’autres sites, ayant d’autres climats, d’autres contextes pédologiques, d’autres pratiques agricoles, et d’autres configurations de réseau de drainage. Les performances des quatre modèles varient entre les sous-bassins AB$_1$ et AB$_2$, laissant penser que sur d’autres sites ces dernières pourraient être différentes (typiquement, SIDRA pourrait être plus performant sur des sites ayant plus de parcelles équipées de drains occasionnant une dynamique de drainage plus réactive). Cela permettrait de recommander l’un ou l’autre modèle en fonction du contexte spécifique du site étudié. - Il serait intéressant d’évaluer les quatre modèles sur d’autres années hydrologiques. Les performances des modèles varient entre 2021 et 2022, notamment parce que l’année 2022 a été marquée par une importante sécheresse, et que la réponse du drainage à l’irrigation appliquée diffère entre les deux années (en 2022, il y a eu moins de drainage alors que plus d’irrigation a été appliquée qu’en 2021). Quelles seraient les performances des modèles sur d’autres années hydrologiques ? Est-ce que pour des années moins sèches que 2022 et plus semblables à 2021, les performances des modèles seraient similaires à celles observées pour l’année 2021 ? Le drainage continue d’être mesuré à AB$_1$ et AB$_2$. Dès qu’un volume de données suffisant sera disponible, il serait intéressant d’évaluer les quatre modèles en utilisant ces dernières. [SOURCE: Page_172]

Cette thèse s’est attachée à développer des approches visant à améliorer le suivi de l’irrigation et du drainage des périmètres irrigués. Ces approches ont été calibrées et validées sur le périmètre irrigué d’AB de 80 km^2 , situé au nord-est de l’Espagne. Les quatre chapitres présentés ont couvert plusieurs sujets, allant de l’analyse de sensibilité du modèle SAMIR (utilisé tout au long de la thèse), en passant par l’assimilation de données (d’abord d’irrigation, puis de données de SSM) dans le modèle SAMIR, pour terminer par la simulation du drainage agricole à l’échelle de sous- bassins irrigués. Dans ce chapitre de conclusion, les quatre travaux présentés dans cette thèse sont résumés, leurs principales limites sont explicitées, et des nouvelles perspectives de recherche sont proposées. Les perspectives à court et moyen termes, directement liées aux méthodologies développées dans cette thèse sont d’abord exposées, suivies des perspectives à long terme. Ces dernières résultent d’une réflexion plus large sur les travaux de la thèse, les situant dans un contexte plus vaste. [SOURCE: Page_173]

## 162                           CHAPITRE 7. CONCLUSION GÉNÉRALE ET PERSPECTIVES

celle-ci a été appliquée sur dix sites différents et un total de 37 saisons agricoles présentant des contextes agro-pédo-climatiques variés. La méthode utilisée s’appelle Sobol, et présente l’avan- tage d’être une méthode d’analyse globale (l’utilisation de ce type de méthode est très fortement recommandée dans la littérature). Elle permet de prendre en compte les variations de l’ensemble des paramètres analysés à la fois, ainsi que leurs interactions. Les résultats obtenus montrent que l’essentiel de la sensibilité de SAMIR se concentre sur seulement deux paramètres (aKcb et Zrmax ). Il apparaı̂t que l’un ou l’autre de ces paramètres est plus ou moins sensible en fonction du stress hydrique que peuvent potentiellement subir les cultures. Un proxy de la sensibilité de SAMIR a alors été proposé, qui se calcule pour un site donné à partir d’une simulation réalisée avec des paramètres moyens. Ce proxy permet de prédire la sensibilité de SAMIR (lequel des deux paramètres est le plus sensible) avec une bonne efficacité, que ce soit pour la simulation de l’ET ou du DP . [SOURCE: Page_174]

La deuxième partie concerne le développement d’une nouvelle approche visant à inverser les paramètres d’irrigation de SAMIR (SMthreshold et Idose ) et permettant ainsi de simuler une irriga- tion réaliste à l’échelle d’un périmètre irrigué. Pour ce faire, des données d’irrigation d’une année spécifique du périmètre irrigué d’AB ont été assimilées dans SAMIR. Le schéma d’assimilation proposé repose sur un filtre particulaire ayant la capacité de fournir des valeurs de SMthreshold et Idose journalières et lissées. Ces paramètres d’irrigation sont, dans un second temps, utilisés pour simuler l’irrigation de chaque parcelle avec SAMIR. Ces irrigations sont ensuite agrégées tem- porellement à l’échelle hebdomadaire et spatialement à celle du périmètre irrigué. Les résultats montrent que l’irrigation hebdomadaire simulée avec cette nouvelle approche permet de très bien reproduire l’irrigation hebdomadaire observée, non seulement sur l’année qui a servi à inverser SMthreshold et Idose , mais aussi sur quatre autres années dédiées à la validation de l’approche. Cela suggère qu’une seule année de données d’irrigation hebdomadaires permet d’extraire les pratiques moyennes des agriculteurs d’un périmètre irrigué, celles-ci ayant une certaine inertie d’une année à l’autre. Cependant, cette approche est confrontée à une limite majeure, étant qu’elle dépend de données d’irrigation qui ne sont qu’exceptionnellement disponibles. [SOURCE: Page_174]

La troisième partie est consacrée à une approche, appelée SSM-ASSIM, qui se propose de dépasser cette limite en assimilant des données satellites de SSM à haute résolution, disponibles facilement, fréquemment (tous les six jours), et en tous lieux. Le schéma d’assimilation développé dans la partie précédente a été utilisé, avec une différence : des valeurs journalières de SMthreshold et de Idose ont été obtenues pour chacun des principaux types de culture du périmètre d’AB. Ces dernières ont alors été appliquées aux parcelles du périmètre d’AB pour y simuler l’irrigation hebdomadaire. Sur l’année 2019, la seule étudiée, l’irrigation hebdomadaire simulée au périmètre d’AB a une dynamique qui correspond de manière satisfaisante à celle de l’irrigation observée. Une surestimation au printemps est toutefois à noter, ainsi qu’une sous-estimation en été, toutes deux étant cependant moindres que celles obtenues par une autre méthode d’inversion de l’irriga- tion à partir de données satellite de SSM (SM2RAIN) sur le même périmètre et la même année. Cette surestimation et cette sous-estimation ont également été observées lorsque SSM-ASSIM a été appliquée sur les deux parcelles instrumentées Albesa et Castello. La dynamique de l’irriga- tion observée y est très bien reproduite, mais une sous-estimation se produit systématiquement au moment où l’irrigation est intense en été. Une légère surestimation de l’irrigation y est égale- ment observée au printemps. [SOURCE: Page_174]

La quatrième partie se concentre sur la simulation du drainage en contexte irrigué. Plus précisément, les performances de quatre modèles parcimonieux de simulation du drainage (RU- Reservoir, RU-SIDRA, SAMIR-Reservoir, SAMIR-SIDRA), ayant de deux à quatre paramètres [SOURCE: Page_174]

## 7.2. LIMITES ET PERSPECTIVES À COURT ET MOYEN TERMES                                                   163

principaux (plus sensibles), ont été évaluées en confrontant leurs simulations à des données de drainage observées aux exutoires de deux sous-bassins (AB$_1$ et AB$_2$) du périmètre d’AB. Ces quatre modèles sont le résultat de la combinaison de deux modèles de surface (RU et SAMIR) et de deux modèles souterrains (Reservoir et SIDRA). Dans un premier temps, leur précision a été évaluée. Par précision, il est entendu ici la capacité des modèles à reproduire le drainage lorsqu’ils sont calibrés sur des données de drainage. Les résultats ont montré que le modèle le plus simple, RU-Reservoir (deux paramètres principaux) est le plus performant pour reproduire le drainage après une étape de calibration. Cette évaluation a permis de mettre en lumière le fait que le modèle Reservoir est plus adapté que SIDRA à la faible réactivité du drainage observé sur les sous-bassins AB$_1$ et AB$_2$. Les modèles basés sur SIDRA pourraient être plus adaptés dans le cas de sous-bassins plus réactifs. Il est également apparu qu’il est important de réaliser les simulations avec un modèle de surface spatialisé à l’échelle de la parcelle, en utilisant en forçage une irrigation spatialisée pour reproduire de manière adéquate la recharge. Dans un second temps, l’exactitude (accuracy) des modèles a été évaluée. Par exactitude, il est entendu ici la capacité des modèles à reproduire le drainage en utilisant des valeurs par défaut issues de la littérature pour calibrer leurs paramètres principaux. On a cherché ici à répondre à la question : ”Dans le cas où il n’y a pas de données de drainage disponibles, quel modèle faudrait-il utiliser pour avoir la meilleure estimation du drainage ?”. Les résultats ont montré que le modèle SAMIR-Reservoir est le plus exact (ou le moins inexact), capable de reproduire grossièrement le drainage mensuel observé à AB$_1$ et AB$_2$ avec des paramètres calibrés par défaut. [SOURCE: Page_175]

7.2     Limites et perspectives à court et moyen termes 7.2.1   Analyse de sensibilité de SAMIR L’analyse de sensibilité de SAMIR a permis de connaı̂tre la sensibilité de ses paramètres et de proposer un proxy permettant de prédire cette dernière sans avoir à réaliser une analyse de sensibilité. Les conclusions principales de l’analyse de sensibilité de SAMIR sont 1) qu’il y a deux groupes de type de sensibilité PHENO et STRESS chacun représentés par un paramètre plus sensible, et 2) que la sensibilité d’un site en particulier peut être identifiée à travers le calcul d’un proxy basé sur le stress hydrique potentiel de la culture étudié. Cela peut s’avérer utile pour limiter au maximum le nombre de paramètres à calibrer, notamment dans le cas d’une spatialisation à large échelle de SAMIR où une calibration spécifique serait effectuée au niveau de chaque parcelle. Une limite de cette analyse est à mentionner. Elle s’est concentrée sur des périodes allant du semis jusqu’à la récolte, durant lesquelles de la végétation est présente, et où il y a le plus d’échanges de flux d’eau agricoles. De ce fait, les conclusions de ce travail s’appliquent unique- ment pour ces périodes, et non sur des périodes d’inter-culture durant lesquelles il peut y avoir une majorité de journées avec du sol nu. Durant les périodes de sol nu, les paramètres liés à l’évaporation sont plus sensibles. Il serait intéressant d’appliquer cette analyse de sensibilité à d’autres modèles basés sur l’approche FAO-2Kc, tels que AquaCrop (Raes et al., 2009) ou SimdualKc (Rolim et al., 2007; Rosa et al., 2012). Cela permettrait de vérifier si les conclusions de notre travail s’appliquent à ces modèles, et finalement, si elles peuvent servir à la compréhension et à l’utilisation de ces derniers. Sans avoir réalisé cette analyse de sensibilité, il aurait été difficile de mettre en œuvre les approches d’assimilation et de calibration de cette thèse. Dans ce cas, il aurait fallu calibrer de nombreux paramètres pour augmenter les chances d’ajuster les plus sensibles, ce qui aurait été difficilement envisageable en termes de coût computationnel. De plus, nous aurions potentielle- [SOURCE: Page_175]

Avant l’analyse de sensibilité présentée ici, l’état de l’art en matière de sensibilité du modèle SAMIR était le travail de Olivera-Guerra et al. (2020). Ils avaient identifié SMF C et SMW P comme étant les paramètres les plus sensibles en effectuant une analyse de sensibilité locale (donc limitée, voir Saltelli et al. 2008, 2010) portant uniquement sur trois paramètres. Si nous avions construit nos travaux en nous appuyant sur cet état de l’art, notre attention aurait été concentrée sur SMF C et SMW P , qui en réalité sont peu sensibles comme nous l’avons montré dans le Chapitre 3. En outre, si SMF C et SMW P avaient effectivement été plus sensibles, il aurait potentiellement été inapproprié d’utiliser les données de sol provenant du produit global SoilGrids, ces dernières comportant des incertitudes liées à leur échelle spatiale. [SOURCE: Page_176]

7.2.2   Inversion de l’irrigation à partir de données d’humidité du sol de surface J’identifie ici certaines limites de l’approche SSM-ASSIM, qui chacune ouvre des perspectives pour son évaluation, son amélioration, et/ou pour mieux la comprendre. [SOURCE: Page_176]

1. À l’échelle du périmètre irrigué, l’approche a été validée sur une seule année hydrologique (2019) et sur un seul site (le périmètre d’AB). À l’échelle de la parcelle, elle a été validée sur seulement quatre saisons agricoles et deux sites (les parcelles Albesa et Castello). Il serait intéressant d’évaluer l’approche sur d’autres sites, variés en termes de texture de sol, de type de culture, de pratique d’irrigation, et de climat. Cela permettrait de valider la robustesse de SSM-ASSIM, et potentiellement de mieux comprendre son fonctionnement. 2. Pour mieux comprendre son fonctionnement, il serait intéressant d’évaluer SSM-ASSIM en réalisant une expérience synthétique, en s’inspirant par exemple du travail de Zappa et al. (2022). Celle-ci pourrait permettre de comprendre l’effet de la fréquence d’observation, des pratiques d’irrigation, du type de culture dominant de la zone étudiée, ou encore de la qualité des données de SSM assimilées, sur les capacités de l’approche à simuler l’irrigation. Cette expérience synthétique pourrait consister en ces différentes étapes : a) Générer artificiellement des séries temporelles d’irrigation (plus ou moins fréquentes et plus ou moins intenses). b) Simuler la SSM avec SAMIR en utilisant ces différentes irrigations en forçage. De plus, simuler une SSM pour différents types de culture afin de comparer les performances obtenues pour différentes cultures. c) Assimiler dans SAMIR les données de SSM synthétiques simulées durant l’étape b). Afin d’évaluer l’impact de la fréquence d’assimilation, une valeur de SSM pourrait être assimilée tous les 1, 2, 3, 6, et 12 jours, par exemple. Il serait également possible de “dégrader” la qualité des données de SSM pour évaluer l’impact de l’incertitude de la SSM sur l’irrigation simulée (en quelque sorte évaluer la propagation de l’erreur de la SSM sur l’irrigation simulée). d) Simuler l’irrigation hebdomadaire avec les séries temporelles de paramètres SMthreshold et Idose retrouvés avec les différents scénarios de pratique d’irrigation / type de culture / qualité de données de SSM / fréquence d’observation, afin d’évaluer l’impact de ces différents facteurs sur l’irrigation. In fine, cela permettrait de mieux comprendre les forces et les faiblesses de la méthode SSM-ASSIM, et de proposer des pistes pour surmonter ses faiblesses. Cela permettrait également de discerner le facteur le plus sensible, le plus important pour la simulation de l’irrigation, étant la principale source d’incertitude dans cette dernière. Cela ouvrirait des pistes pour réduire l’incertitude associée à ce facteur plus important. [SOURCE: Page_176]

## 7.2. LIMITES ET PERSPECTIVES À COURT ET MOYEN TERMES                                                165

3. SSM-ASSIM a du mal à reproduire d’importantes quantités d’irrigation en été (typique- ment lorsqu’elles sont supérieures à 50 mm/semaine). Cette sous-estimation provient du fait que la relation entre la SSM et l’irrigation est non linéaire : au-delà d’une certaine valeur de SSM, le signal de l’irrigation est moins apparent dans la SSM. Pour réduire cette sous-estimation, il serait envisageable de modifier le formalisme de SAMIR, et notamment sa manière de simuler la SSM. Une piste pourrait être de faire en sorte que la SSM simulée puisse atteindre des valeurs correspondantes à celle d’une humidité à saturation (actuelle- ment la SSM est limitée à SMF C dans SAMIR), et de simuler la SSM en tenant compte des processus d’infiltration qui ont lieu à une humidité supérieure à SMF C . Avec un tel formalisme, pour maintenir une SSM élevée avec SAMIR, il faudrait simuler des irrigations plus fréquentes et/ou plus intenses. La sous-estimation de l’irrigation dans les moments où la SSM assimilée est élevée pourrait alors être réduite. 4. Une autre limite réside dans la qualité du produit satellite de SSM utilisé. Par exemple, la surestimation importante de l’irrigation observée au printemps avec SSM-ASSIM au périmètre d’AB pourrait provenir de la qualité des données satellites de SSM. En effet, cette surestimation provient d’une augmentation soudaine de la SSM début mai 2019, alors que l’on aurait pu s’attendre à une augmentation de la SSM moins abrupte du fait que l’irrigation avait déjà commencé mi-avril 2019. En outre, nous avons vu que l’algorithme d’inversion de la SSM satellite utilisé rencontre des difficultés à détecter l’augmentation de la SSM au début de la saison estivale, lorsque les agriculteurs pratiquent du semi- direct en laissant des tiges entre deux cultures (ces dernières sont interprétées comme de la végétation par l’algorithme WCM). Toute amélioration de la SSM satellite assimilée aurait une conséquence directe sur les performances de l’approche SSM-ASSIM. 5. Un moyen d’améliorer les performances et d’assurer une plus grande robustesse de l’ap- proche SSM-ASSIM serait d’assimiler des données satellites d’ET en plus des données de SSM. En effet, tout comme la SSM, l’ET contient une information sur le signal d’irriga- tion du fait qu’elle est directement régie par la disponibilité en eau dans la zone racinaire. Cependant, l’ET , contrairement à la SSM, ne contient pas d’information sur l’excès d’ir- rigation (qui engendre de la DP et du drainage). Cela s’explique par le fait que la valeur maximale de l’ET observée correspond à la quantité maximale d’eau que la culture peut consommer, en plus d’une part d’évaporation du sol, et que cette quantité maximale est déterminée par les conditions atmosphériques, c’est-à-dire la demande évaporative. Des produits satellitaires d’ET existent d’ores et déjà à des échelles spatiales intéressantes (par exemple le produit Sen^4ET qui combine les données des capteurs S$_2$ et Sentinel-3, avec une résolution de 10 mètres et une revisite de 10 jours ; Guzinski et al. 2020). D’autres missions satellites vont être lancées ces prochaines années, et fourniront des produits d’ET de meilleure qualité, et à plus haute résolution spatiale et temporelle : Thermal infraRed Imaging Satellite for High-resolution Natural resource Assessment (TRISHNA ; Lagouarde et al. 2018) fournira des données d’ET avec une résolution spatiale d’environ 50 mètres et une fréquence de trois jours, et Land Surface Temperature Monitoring (LSTM ; Koetz et al. 2018) fournira des données d’une résolution d’environ 50 mètres également avec une fréquence de 1 à 3 jours. En outre, plusieurs travaux ont déjà assimilé des données d’ET dans des modèles de bilan d’eau des cultures ou de surface terrestre pour retrouver l’irri- gation (par exemple, Vogels et al. 2020; Anderson et al. 2015; López Valencia et al. 2020). L’ajout de l’ET dans le schéma d’assimilation SSM-ASSIM pourrait s’appuyer sur cet état de l’art. Ce travail de recherche a été récemment proposé dans le cadre d’une réponse à un appel d’offres du CNES financé par le plan France 2030. 6.
